title: The Decalogue as a Charter Against War, Plunder, and Oppression
article_text:
This paper argues that the Decalogue—the Ten Commandments of the Hebrew Bible (Exodus 20:2–17; Deuteronomy 5:6–21)—together with its striking parallels in the Quranic ethical corpus (6:151–153; 17:22–39; 2:83; 4:36; 5:32; 16:90) and the radical humanist teachings of Jesus of Nazareth (Matthew 5–7; 19:16–19; 22:37–40; Mark 10:17–19; Luke 10:25–28), constitutes the most enduring and universal charter against war (cf. Exodus 20:13; Deuteronomy 5:17; Matthew 5:9, 5:21–22; Quran 5:32), looting and the plunder of resources (Exodus 20:15; Deuteronomy 5:19; Matthew 19:18; Quran 2:188; 4:29), killing (Exodus 20:13; Deuteronomy 5:17; Matthew 5:21–22; Quran 6:151; 17:33), the theft and unjust appropriation of natural wealth (Quran 7:85; 11:85; 26:183), sexual violence and exploitation, particularly against women in conditions of vulnerability (Exodus 20:14; Deuteronomy 5:18; Matthew 5:27–28; Quran 17:32; 24:30–33; 4:19), and diplomatic deception and false testimony (Exodus 20:16; Deuteronomy 5:20; Matthew 5:33–37; Quran 2:42; 16:105; 24:7–9).
This paper re-reads these ancient moral imperatives through the lens of contemporary neuroscience, evolutionary biology, sociology, and peace studies. It contends that the Decalogue is not a relic of ancient tribal theocracy but a “beta code” for human liberation – a cognitive, social, and spiritual architecture designed to prevent ontological violence and foster genuine human flourishing. By integrating scriptural analysis with the latest findings of Robert Sapolsky, Martha Nussbaum, Johan Galtung, Amartya Sen, and others, this paper advances a humanistic synthesis capable of grounding arguments against war-mongers, religious fanatics, and political fundamentalists on foundations that are simultaneously ancient and scientifically robust. The Decalogue, properly understood, is not the property of any single religion; it is the moral grammar of a species that wishes to survive.
The Moral Structure of a World in Crisis
In the spring of 2026, the world presents a spectacle that would have been recognisable to the authors of the Book of Exodus. Nations are arrayed against nations; civilians flee burning cities; oil fields are seized under the cover of military action; women are raped as a systematic instrument of war; and the chambers of diplomacy echo with sophisticated lies dressed in the language of international law. The technological apparatus of civilisation – satellites, algorithms, financial instruments, nuclear arsenals – is immeasurably more advanced than anything the ancient world imagined. And yet the moral failures on display are identical to those that prompted the most ancient law codes in human history.
This paper contends that this coincidence is not accidental. The moral pathologies that drive modern warfare – the idolatry of national power, the dehumanisation of the enemy, the unchecked appetite for resources, the instrumentalisation of women’s bodies as weapons, the weaponisation of truth itself – are precisely the pathologies that the Decalogue, the Quranic ethical catalogue, and the teachings of Jesus were designed to diagnose and cure. These are not three separate moral systems competing for adherents. They are three articulations of the same deep structure of human social requirements, each adapted to a specific historical and cultural context, but each pointing toward the same horizon: a world free from ontological violence, structured by justice, and animated by the love of the neighbour.
The central argument of this work is deceptively simple. Human beings are, in the language of evolutionary biology, obligate social animals. Our survival as a species depends upon our ability to cooperate in groups, and sustained cooperation is impossible without trust. Trust, in turn, is impossible in the absence of the moral commitments encoded in the Decalogue: do not kill your fellow human beings arbitrarily; do not steal what belongs to others; do not bear false witness; do not consume your neighbours with covetous desire. These are not arbitrary divine commands; they are, as neuroscience now confirms, the formalised conditions of our biological flourishing (Sapolsky, p.24). When nations violate them on a mass scale – as happens in every modern war – they are not merely sinning in a theological sense; they are attacking the biological and psychological infrastructure of the human species itself.
This paper proceeds in ten substantive sections. It begins with the foundational preamble of the Decalogue, which locates all moral law within the prior act of liberation. It then addresses, in turn, the specific contemporary crises of killing and warfare, resource looting and oil theft, sexual violence against women, and deception in international affairs. It examines religious fanaticism and fundamentalism as a modern form of the idolatry condemned in the first three commandments. It reviews the scientific evidence for the biology of violence and the biology of peace. It reflects on the Sabbath principle as a pointer toward ecological and human sustainability. It concludes with a vision of justice, peace, and flourishing drawn from the synthesis of the ancient moral codes and the most current findings of the human sciences.
A note on method: this paper reads the Decalogue and its Quranic and Christian parallels through what may be termed a “Quranic humanistic lens.” This does not mean that the analysis is confined to Islamic thought, nor that it is in any way dismissive of other traditions. Rather, it means that the specific Quranic articulations of the moral imperatives – with their emphasis on Adl (justice), Ihsan (excellence), Mizan (balance), and Karama (inherent dignity) – provide a unique and inclusive framework for the synthesis attempted here. The Quran speaks to the entirety of humanity as “the children of Adam” (17:70), and it is in that universal spirit that this work proceeds.
The Exodus Preamble: Liberation as the Prerequisite of Law
The Decalogue does not begin with a command. It begins with an announcement: “I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery” (Exod. 20.2). This preamble is the hermeneutical key to the entire document. Before the first imperative is issued, a prior act of liberation is declared. The law is not imposed upon slaves; it is offered to free people. This sequencing is theologically and politically decisive.
In the ancient world, Pharaoh’s Egypt was the paradigmatic extraction state. Slaves were human beings reduced entirely to their productive utility. There was no Sabbath under Pharaoh; there was only the quota of bricks. The Decalogue, as the theologian Walter Brueggemann has argued, is at its very foundation an “anti-Pharaoh” document – a constitution for a community that has been liberated from the logic of pure extraction and must now learn to live otherwise (Brueggemann, p.3). The moral law is the social form that liberated life takes when it refuses to replicate the systems of its oppressors.
This preamble has direct and urgent implications for contemporary warfare. Every modern war is, in some fundamental sense, a reassertion of Pharaoh’s logic. It is the attempt by one power to reduce another people – and other people’s land, resources, and women – to instruments of its own will. When a nation invades another to seize its oil, it is re-enacting the slavery of Egypt in a modern key: it is saying that the people of that land are not subjects with inalienable rights but objects whose resources can be expropriated by superior force. When armies systematically rape women in occupied territories, they are asserting precisely the logic of the slave-master: that the bodies of the conquered are the property of the conqueror. The Decalogue was written against this logic. Its preamble insists that human beings are, first and foremost, liberated subjects – never the property of another power.
The Quranic resonance is profound. The Quranic ethical catalogue in Q.6:151-153 and 17:23-39 presents moral imperatives as “Hikmah” – Wisdom – and as the “Straight Path” for a community emerging from the chaos and tribalism of the pre-Islamic era. Just as the Biblical Decalogue follows the escape from bondage, the Quranic mandates offer a framework for maintaining the integrity of a community that has moved beyond the “Jahiliyyah” – the era of ignorance and tribal violence. In both traditions, the moral law is the scaffold upon which a liberated society is built. Without it, freedom degenerates either into the anarchy of “every man for himself” or into the tyranny of “the strongest man for all.”
The implications for contemporary political philosophy are clear. No state, however powerful, can claim the right to re-impose the logic of Pharaoh upon other peoples. International law, at its best, is an attempt to codify this Exodus preamble in secular terms: it asserts that the sovereignty of every people is prior to the power of any invading force, just as the freedom of the liberated community is prior to the commands of the law. When war-mongers invoke “national interest” or “security imperatives” to justify conquest, they are speaking the language of Pharaoh. The Decalogue answers them from its very first line.
Against Killing: The Sanctity of Life in an Age of Perpetual War
The Sixth Commandment – “You shall not murder” (Exodus 20.13) – is the bedrock of any viable social contract. Yet it is also the commandment most systematically violated by the modern state in its conduct of war. The history of the twentieth and twenty-first centuries is, in significant part, a history of the industrialisation of killing: from the trenches of the Somme to the gas chambers of Auschwitz, from the atomic obliteration of Hiroshima to the drone strikes of the global war on terror, from the machetes of Rwanda to the barrel bombs of Syria. What makes this history so morally instructive – and so tragic – is that virtually every episode of mass killing has been accompanied by sophisticated moral justifications: self-defence, civilisational necessity, religious duty, ethnic survival, pre-emptive security. The perpetrators of mass violence are almost never cynics. They are, as Robert Sapolsky’s landmark work demonstrates, human beings whose capacity for dehumanisation has been activated by the particular combination of ideology, fear, and social pressure (Sapolsky, p.490).
The Quranic elaboration of this commandment is among the most powerful statements of the sanctity of life in any religious literature. The Quran states: “Whoever kills a soul unless for a soul or for corruption in the land – it is as if he had slain all of mankind. And whoever saves one – it is as if he had saved all of mankind” (5:32). This is not merely a moral sentiment; it is an ontological claim. Each human life is presented as a microcosm of the whole – a unique and irreplaceable expression of the human family. To destroy it is not merely to harm an individual; it is to rupture the entire fabric of the species.
This Quranic universalisation of the soul is the definitive refutation of the logic of dehumanisation. Every act of mass killing in history has been preceded by a process of symbolic degradation: the victim group is labelled as less than human – as “cockroaches,” as “vermin,” as “infidels,” as “collateral damage.” The anthropologist Michael Taussig has called this “the magic of the state” – the ability of political authority to transform persons into objects through the alchemy of language (Quoted in Sapolsky, p.555). The Decalogue’s Sixth Commandment and the Quranic elaboration of 5:32 are a direct counter-magic: they re-person the victim, insisting that every life destroyed is a universe destroyed.
Contemporary neuroscience provides a compelling biological corroboration. Sapolsky’s research demonstrates that the human capacity for empathy is biologically real and neurologically instantiated. The mirror neuron system allows human beings to simulate the pain and experience of others within their own nervous systems (Sapolsky, p.575). Crucially, however, this empathic capacity is profoundly susceptible to manipulation. When a person is categorised as “Other” – as a member of a different ethnic, religious, or national group – the empathic response is diminished or suppressed altogether. The ideological work of war is precisely the work of suppressing empathy: of making it cognitively and emotionally possible to kill people whom, in any other context, one would recognise as persons. The moral counter-technology of the Sixth Commandment is the insistence that this suppression is illegitimate: the neighbour, however defined, remains a person, and persons may not be killed.
Jesus radicalises this commandment by tracing the root of murder to its psychological antecedent: “You have heard that it was said to those of old, You shall not murder… But I say to you that everyone who is angry with his brother will be liable to judgement” (Matt. 5.21-22). This is a remarkable anticipatory insight into the social psychology of violence. The neurobiological chain from angry contempt to physical aggression is well-documented in the literature (Goleman, p.59). Jesus targets the chain at its earliest link. A civilisation that wishes to prevent war must cultivate the internal dispositions that make war psychologically impossible: the recognition of the full humanity of every person, the discipline of empathy over contempt, and the practice of conflict resolution through dialogue rather than domination.
For contemporary war-mongers, religious or secular, the answer of the Decalogue and its parallels is unambiguous: no cause, however sacred it is proclaimed to be, justifies the mass killing of civilians. No oil field, no border dispute, no theological disagreement, no perceived humiliation of national honour, licenses the industrialised destruction of human lives. The Sixth Commandment is absolute in the most humanistic sense of the word: it is grounded not in an arbitrary divine decree but in the biological and ontological reality that every human life is a universe, and its destruction is a crime against the species as a whole.
The Plunder of Nations: Oil Theft, Economic Looting, and the Eighth Commandment
The Eighth Commandment – “You shall not steal” (Exodus 20.15) – has, in the context of modern international relations, an application that its original framers could not have imagined: the systematic theft of an entire nation’s natural resources under the cover of military occupation or economic coercion. In the twenty-first century, the most conspicuous form of large-scale theft is the seizure or exploitation of oil – the fossil fuel that underwrites modern industrial civilisation and that has, accordingly, become the most fought-over commodity in human history. The wars in Iraq, Libya, Sudan, and the South China Sea, the geopolitical manoeuvring around the Caspian Basin and the Gulf states, the sanctions regimes designed to exclude certain nations from the revenues of their own resources – all of these are expressions, in one form or another, of the violation of the Eighth Commandment at the level of the international order.
The Quranic parallel is remarkably specific. In the Quran, the ethical mandate extends from the personal prohibition of theft to an explicit requirement of institutional integrity in the distribution of resources: “And do not approach the property of the orphan except in the way that is best… and give full measure and weight in justice” (6:152). The “orphan” in the ancient context was the paradigmatic non-person – someone with legal rights but no power to enforce them. In the modern context, the “orphan” is the citizen of a nation whose sovereignty is nominal but whose resources are extracted by more powerful actors through the mechanisms of debt, military occupation, asymmetric trade agreements, or outright conquest. The Quranic insistence on “full measure and weight in justice” is a demand for institutional integrity in the international economic order.
Amartya Sen’s “Capabilities Approach” provides the contemporary philosophical framework for understanding why resource theft is a moral catastrophe of the first order (Sen, p.3). Sen argues that economic development is, at its core, a process of expanding the real freedoms that people enjoy – their ability to live long and healthy lives, to access education, to participate in political life, and to exercise the basic functions of human dignity. When a nation’s oil or mineral wealth is seized by an occupying power or extracted through a system of exploitative contracts, the consequence is not merely an accounting loss. It is the destruction of the capability base of an entire generation. The schools that could have been built, the hospitals that could have been staffed, the public infrastructure that could have been maintained – all of these are the victims of resource theft. It is a form of slow-motion killing as lethal as the Sixth Commandment’s prohibition of murder, differing only in the time scale of its violence.
David Graeber’s study of the history of debt illuminates a related mechanism of structural theft: the use of international financial instruments – debt, interest, structural adjustment conditionality – to extract value from poorer nations and transfer it to wealthier ones (Graeber, p.12). This is the contemporary equivalent of the Quranic prohibition of Riba (usury) – the categorical condemnation of systems that allow capital to multiply without genuine productive contribution, while placing the burden of compounding repayment upon the debtor. When an international financial institution imposes austerity conditions upon a nation in exchange for emergency loans, compelling it to sell its natural assets at distressed prices, it is committing a form of institutional usury that the Quranic ethical system identifies as a profound violation of justice.
The neuro-economics of fairness provides the scientific counterpart to this moral argument. Research using the “Ultimatum Game” – a laboratory paradigm in which subjects can accept or reject a proposed division of resources – consistently demonstrates that human beings have an evolved “Fairness Instinct.” When the division is perceived as grossly unjust, subjects reject the offer even at personal cost, triggering a response in the anterior insula – the region of the brain associated with the experience of disgust (Sapolsky, p.490). This biological response to unfairness is the evolutionary substrate of the moral sense: it is the neurological echo of the Eighth Commandment, a deep somatic protest against the violation of fair measure. It suggests that the outrage of nations subjected to resource imperialism is not merely political; it is a biological response to the violation of a universal human norm.
The Quranic concept of Khilafa (Stewardship) provides the positive corollary to the prohibition of theft. If the Earth and its resources are held in trust for the whole of humanity – including future generations – then no single state or corporate entity can claim absolute ownership of a nation’s subsoil assets. The human being is a “Khalifa” – a trustee – not an owner whose rights of extraction and destruction are unlimited. This principle of stewardship over ownership is the ethical foundation for the emerging body of international environmental law, which increasingly recognises that the resources of the natural world are a “common heritage of mankind” rather than the private property of whoever happens to have the military power to occupy the terrain above them.
Gender Violence, Sacred Dignity, and the Seventh Commandment
Among the most ancient and most persistent war crimes is the systematic sexual violation of women by occupying or invading forces. The rape of women in war is not an aberration or an accident of conflict; it is, as the documentation of the International Criminal Court and the United Nations Security Council resolutions on “Women, Peace and Security” have established, a deliberate weapon of war, a tactic of ethnic cleansing, a mechanism of social domination, and a symbolic assertion of the conqueror’s absolute power over the conquered (UN Security Council Res. 1325). In Bosnia, Rwanda, the Democratic Republic of Congo, and Iraq, mass sexual violence has been prosecuted – too rarely, too slowly, and with too few convictions – as a crime against humanity. It is also, this paper argues, a categorical violation of the Seventh, Fifth, and Sixth Commandments simultaneously: it destroys the person, it desecrates the covenant of bodily integrity, and it murders the dignity that makes human life worth living.
The Seventh Commandment – “You shall not commit adultery” (Exodus 20.14) – is, in its humanistic reading, a protection of “Relational Integrity” and the “Sanctity of Consent.” Read in the context of wartime sexual violence, it takes on a dimension of terrible urgency. Rape is not adultery in the conventional legal sense; it is the violent destruction of the very capacity for consensual relationship. A humanistic reading of the Seventh Commandment must therefore encompass the absolute prohibition of all non-consensual sexual acts, since the commandment’s deepest purpose is to protect the “Relational Commons” – the space of trust and mutual vulnerability in which genuine human bonds are formed.
The Quranic parallel is notably preventive: “And do not go near adultery; indeed, it is an indecency and an evil way” (17:32). The phrase “do not go near” establishes a proactive ethics of protection rather than a merely reactive prohibition. In the context of war, “going near adultery” encompasses the entire culture of militarism that treats women’s bodies as spoils of conquest – the propaganda that dehumanises the enemy’s women, the command cultures that turn a blind eye to sexual violence, the social impunity that makes prosecution rare and conviction rarer still. The Quranic imperative demands that we address these preconditions of violation, not merely the act itself.
The Quranic anthropology of the “Single Soul” (Nafsin Wahidah) provides the deepest foundation for the moral argument against wartime sexual violence (Quran 4:1). If all of humanity shares a single creational origin – if the woman in the occupied territory is, in the most fundamental ontological sense, made of the same substance as the soldier who violates her – then the act of rape is a violation not merely of another person but of one’s own essential nature. It is a form of ontological self-destruction, a rupture in the “Single Soul” of the species. The Islamic feminist scholar Amina Wadud has argued that this “Tawhidic paradigm” of the Quran demands the absolute equality and dignity of all human beings, and that any claim of the right to dominate or violate another person on the basis of gender, ethnicity, or conquest constitutes a form of Shirk – the idolatrous elevation of the self over the divine standard of justice (Wadud, p.34).
Contemporary neurobiology confirms the catastrophic and lasting damage of sexual violence. Trauma research documents that the experience of rape – particularly in the context of war, where it is typically public, repeated, and stripped of any possibility of help – produces severe and enduring dysregulation of the body’s stress-response systems, including hyperactivation of the amygdala and suppression of prefrontal cortical function (Sapolsky, p.204). The long-term consequences include post-traumatic stress disorder, chronic depression, social withdrawal, and the transmission of trauma across generations through epigenetic mechanisms. Sexual violence is thus a form of biological warfare: it does not merely harm the individual victim but damages the neurobiological foundations of entire communities, making the intergenerational transmission of the wound a certainty without sustained, expert intervention.
Jesus’ interactions with women in the New Testament offer a consistent model of what the “fulfilment” of the Seventh Commandment looks like in practice. When he declines to condemn the woman brought before him by her accusers, he is not condoning the act; he is refusing to participate in the use of a woman’s body as the site of a political contest between factions of men. He restores her as a subject – a person with a future – rather than allowing her to remain an object of male definition. This “radical personalism,” as this paper terms it, is the positive content of the Seventh Commandment’s prohibition: the active recognition of every person’s inviolable subjectivity, which makes sexual violence, in any form, under any pretext, absolutely inadmissible.
Deceit in International Affairs: False Witness and the Crisis of Global Trust
The Ninth Commandment – “You shall not bear false witness against your neighbour” (Exodus. 20.16) – has, in the twenty-first century, assumed a geopolitical importance that its ancient framers could not have anticipated. We live in an era of systematic state-sponsored deception: manufactured pretexts for war, fabricated intelligence reports, algorithmic disinformation campaigns, “deepfake” video evidence, diplomatic bad faith, and the routine exploitation of international legal language to disguise aggressive intent. The “weapons of mass destruction” that justified the invasion of Iraq in 2003, the “humanitarian intervention” narratives that have masked resource seizure in various theatres of conflict, the elaborate infrastructure of “active measures” by which powerful states subvert the democratic processes of their neighbours – these are all, in the language of the Decalogue, “false witness.” They are systematic lies told at the highest level of the international order, with consequences measured in hundreds of thousands of deaths.
The legal philosopher John Rawls argued that the stability of a just society depends on “Public Reason” – the ability of citizens to debate and decide on the basis of shared facts and logical inferences (Rawls, p.212). Without a shared commitment to the Ninth Commandment, public reason collapses into “tribal rhetoric,” where the goal of speech is not to report reality but to signal loyalty, manufacture consent, or destroy the credibility of the opponent. This is the condition of much international discourse in 2026: a state of “epistemic war” in which the first casualty is not merely truth in the abstract but the specific human lives that depend on accurate information for their survival.
Beyond its legal implications, the Ninth Commandment acts as a fundamental ethical bulwark against the architecture of hatred campaigns by demanding absolute integrity in both public and private discourse. While often interpreted within a narrow judicial context, the prohibition of false witness is more broadly a mandate against any misrepresentation of reality that harms another. It targets the “engines” of hatred—backbiting, tale-bearing, and the intentional spreading of damaging information—which rely on what may be termed “selective reasoning.”
In the lead-up to conflict, propagandists employ selective reasoning through three primary mechanisms: first, they isolate and exaggerate, highlighting negative hearsay while suppressing broader context; second, they generalize accusations, applying an individual’s perceived fault to an entire ethnic or national group; and third, they invent motives, attributing malevolence to neutral actions to “demonize” the neighbour.
The Decalogue directly combats these mechanisms through the “Whole Truth” Principle. By forbidding the circulation of false reports, the commandment implies an affirmative duty to speak the truth in its entirety, thereby destroying the fragmented context necessary for hate speech. This is deeply linked to the “Love Commandment”; because slander is inherently unloving, the Ninth Commandment serves as a covenantal obligation to protect the neighbour’s dignity.
Furthermore, this prohibition serves a crucial sociological function by preventing the “Bandwagon Effect.” It requires individuals to resist joining a “multitude to do evil” (Exodus 23:2) or spreading popular but malicious gossip, demanding instead an independent, truth-based judgment. As Proverbs 6:16-19 suggests, the “false witness who breathes out lies” is an abomination not merely because of the damage to reputation, but because such deceit reflects a character antithetical to the Truth. Ultimately, false witness is a corrosive force that dissolves the trust and social fabric essential for any functional society, making its prohibition a prerequisite for peace.
The Quranic contribution to this epistemic ethics is, as noted in the introduction, among the most radical in any religious literature. The Quran commands: “O you who believe, stand firm for justice as witnesses for God, even if it be against yourselves, or your parents, or your close relatives” (4:135). This is the definitive refutation of the tribalism that underlies most geopolitical deception. The requirement to testify truthfully even against oneself – even against one’s own nation, one’s own government, one’s own side in a conflict – is an extraordinarily demanding standard. It is, however, the only standard that makes international law genuinely possible rather than merely performative. A world in which states can routinely lie at the Security Council, in which intelligence agencies can fabricate the evidence for war, in which military communiques bear no systematic relationship to events on the ground, is a world in which the Rule of Law has become a charade.
The Quran adds a personal dimension of remarkable specificity: “And when you speak, be just, even if it be against a relative” (6:152). The demand for impartial truth – truth that overrides loyalty to the tribe, the party, the nation, the religion – is the foundational principle not only of the scientific method and the rule of law but of civilised international relations. Every diplomat who deliberately misrepresents facts at a negotiating table, every head of state who knowingly fabricates a casus belli, every propagandist who manufactures stories of the enemy’s atrocities to justify the commission of one’s own – each is violating this commandment. And the consequences, as the history of the past century demonstrates with terrible clarity, are not abstract. They are measured in the bodies of the dead.
Jesus distilled the Ninth Commandment into a principle of character rather than merely of conduct: “Let your Yes be Yes and your No be No” (Matt. 5.37). The implication is that truth-telling is not a matter of contractual obligation or legal constraint; it is an expression of the coherence of the self. A person whose inner reality matches their outer speech – whose “witness” is reliable because they have made the alignment of truth and language a matter of personal integrity – is the human foundation upon which any just social order must be built. At the level of international affairs, this translates into the requirement for “epistemic institutions” – free press, independent courts, genuine multilateral oversight, algorithmic transparency – that make it structurally difficult to bear false witness at scale.
The cognitive science of deception confirms the social costs of normalised lying. Leon Festinger’s research on cognitive dissonance shows that the maintenance of systematic deception requires enormous psychological resources and produces chronic stress (Festinger, p.42). Robert Putnam’s research on social capital demonstrates that societies with high levels of honesty and transparency consistently outperform those characterised by pervasive distrust in every measure of human flourishing – economic productivity, democratic stability, public health, and subjective well-being (Putnam, p.135). When states normalise deception in their international conduct, they do not merely harm their adversaries; they degrade the epistemic environment upon which their own citizens’ capacity for self-governance depends. The Ninth Commandment is not only a moral requirement; it is a public health mandate for the species.
Idolatry as Violence: Religious Fanaticism, Fundamentalism, and the First Tablet
Among the most urgent applications of the Decalogue to the contemporary world is its first and foundational cluster of commandments – the prohibition of idolatry and the demand for exclusive loyalty to the transcendent source of justice. For the purposes of this paper, “idolatry” is understood not in the narrowly theological sense of worshipping stone statues but in its broader humanistic sense: the elevation of any finite, human-made reality – a nation, a race, an ethnicity, an interpretation of scripture, a political ideology, a charismatic leader – to the status of an absolute, which then acquires the right to determine who lives and who dies.
In this humanistic sense, violent religious fundamentalism is itself a form of idolatry. It is the elevation of a particular community’s interpretation of the divine will to the status of an unchallengeable absolute, which then licenses the killing of those who disagree. The scholar Khaled Abou El Fadl has argued, in his account of the “Great Theft” of Islam from its humanistic interpreters, that the violent extremism associated with certain strands of contemporary Islamism is not an authentic expression of the Quranic tradition but a profound distortion of it – precisely because it commits the sin of Shirk by placing the absolute authority of the state, the group, or the leader where only the transcendent can legitimately stand (Abou El Fadl, p.82). The same critique applies, with appropriate variations, to Christian fundamentalism, Hindu nationalism, Buddhist chauvinism, and every other form of religious violence: each represents the usurpation of the divine by the human.
The First Commandment – “You shall have no other gods before me” (Exodus 20.3) – is, in its humanistic reading, a declaration of independence for the human conscience from all totalising human authority. By asserting that only the transcendent source of justice and mercy is ultimate, the Decalogue effectively strips every human institution, every political party, every religious community, every charismatic leader of the right to claim absolute obedience. Theodor Adorno’s research on the “Authoritarian Personality” demonstrates that human beings are biologically prone to leader-worship, particularly in times of social crisis (Adorno, p.154). The First Commandment is a cognitive vaccine against this tendency. It tells us that no human being is worthy of the absolute devotion that fanatics give to their leaders and their movements.
The Second Commandment – the prohibition of graven images – extends this critique to conceptual idols. In the modern world, the most dangerous conceptual idols are not carved from wood or stone but from ideology. The nation-state, when it claims that its interests override the universal requirements of justice, becomes an idol. The “pure” ethnic or religious community, when it claims that its survival justifies the elimination of the impure, becomes an idol. The “true” interpretation of scripture, when it claims to possess a certainty so absolute that it licenses violence against those who interpret differently, becomes an idol. Jonathan Haidt’s research on moral psychology demonstrates that human beings are natural-born “groupish” creatures who find it neurologically easy to sanctify their own group and demonise others (Haidt, p.262). The Second Commandment is the counter-move: a standing injunction against the sacralisation of the in-group and the demonisation of the out-group.
The Third Commandment – the prohibition of taking the divine name “in vain” – is the specific prohibition against weaponising the sacred. When religious leaders invoke the name of God to justify mass violence, to sanction the rape of enemy women, to bless the seizure of another people’s oil, or to legitimise diplomatic deception, they are not exercising religious authority; they are committing what this commandment identifies as the most fundamental form of blasphemy. The Quranic parallel – the condemnation of those who “sell God’s signs for a small price” (2:41) – makes explicit that the misuse of sacred language for political or violent ends is a betrayal of the very tradition in the name of which it is perpetrated. A true humanistic monotheism, as both the Decalogue and the Quran conceive it, cannot be weaponised: The God who commands “do not murder” cannot simultaneously command murder, and any tradition that claims otherwise has replaced the living transcendent with a human-made idol wearing the disguise of the divine.
For the war-monger who claims religious sanction, for the fundamentalist who kills in the name of the sacred, for the fanatic who demands absolute loyalty to the group, the message of the Decalogue’s First Tablet is simple and unambiguous: you have made your cause your god. You have committed Shirk. You are not fighting for the divine; you are fighting for your own image of the divine, which is precisely what the First, Second, and Third Commandments forbid. And because you have replaced the transcendent source of justice and mercy with a human-made absolute, you have also lost the only standard by which your violence could ever be justified – because the transcendent source of justice does not justify the murder of the innocent, the theft of the weak, or the rape of the powerless. It forbids them, absolutely, in the very commands that inaugurate moral life.
The Neuroscience of Violence and the Biology of Peace
One of the most significant developments in the scientific literature of the past three decades is the convergence of neuroscience, evolutionary biology, and social psychology around a single, profoundly hopeful conclusion: human beings are not, at their deepest biological level, primarily aggressive. We are, as the evolutionary biologists Samuel Bowles and Herbert Gintis have demonstrated, a “Cooperative Species” whose survival has depended, for the overwhelming majority of our evolutionary history, on our ability to build and sustain high-trust social groups (Bowles and Gintis, p.15). The capacity for violence is real and is not to be minimised; but it is, as Sapolsky’s comprehensive review of the neurobiological evidence demonstrates, always a contextually triggered exception to a more fundamental orientation toward pro-sociality (Sapolsky, p.24).
This scientific insight has direct and important implications for the argument of this paper. If the Decalogue and its Quranic and Christian parallels encode the conditions under which human pro-sociality flourishes – if they are, in biological terms, formalisations of the cooperative norms that allowed our species to survive and evolve – then the violation of these commandments by war-mongers and religious extremists is not merely a moral failure. It is a biological attack on the species’ own survival mechanisms. War, resource theft, sexual violence, and deception are not expressions of deep human nature; they are pathological departures from it, made possible by the specific social and ideological conditions that the Decalogue was designed to prevent.
The neurobiological evidence for the “Love Commandment” of Jesus is particularly striking. Paul Zak’s research into the hormone oxytocin has demonstrated that it is the biological substrate of trust, generosity, and social bonding (Zak, p.52). Acts of kindness – what the Quran calls Ihsan, “doing what is beautiful” – trigger oxytocin release, which in turn reduces the amygdala’s fear response and promotes the prosocial behaviours that sustain high-trust societies. Conversely, conditions of systemic injustice, violence, and deception suppress oxytocin production and elevate cortisol – the stress hormone associated with the “fight or flight” response – creating a neurobiological environment in which violence becomes more likely, trust becomes harder to sustain, and the social fabric continues to fray. In short: The Decalogue is a programme for optimising the neurochemistry of civilisation. Following its precepts is, in a very literal sense, good for our brains.
Johan Galtung’s distinction between “Negative Peace” (the mere absence of direct violence) and “Positive Peace” (the presence of social justice, institutional integrity, and horizontal empathy) provides the peace studies framework that gives scientific content to the vision of “flourishing” that animates this paper (Galtung, p.167). Negative Peace is what the Second Tablet of the Decalogue, taken in isolation, produces: a world in which people refrain from killing and stealing each other. Positive Peace is what the Love Commandment of Jesus and the Quranic Ihsan principle add: a world in which people actively invest in one another’s flourishing, building the social capital that makes genuine, durable, and just peace possible.
The Richard Wilkinson and Kate Pickett study of the relationship between inequality and social outcomes provides perhaps the most powerful empirical demonstration of why the economic commandments of the Decalogue – against theft, against the exploitation of the orphan, against usury – are prerequisites not merely for justice but for the basic public health of a society. Comparing data across twenty-three developed nations, Wilkinson and Pickett demonstrate that more unequal societies consistently have higher rates of violence, lower life expectancy, higher rates of mental illness, lower levels of trust, and weaker educational outcomes – regardless of their average level of wealth (Wilkinson and Pickett 20). Equality is not a luxury; it is a biological necessity. And the moral architecture that the Decalogue provides – fair measure, protection of the orphan, prohibition of theft – is the institutional form that biological necessity takes when a society chooses to live by the grain of its own nature.
The Sabbath Principle: Sustainability, Rest, and Ecological Justice
The Fourth Commandment – “Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy” (Exod. 20.8) – is, at first glance, the most distant from the contemporary crises of war, oil theft, sexual violence, and diplomatic deception. In fact, as this section argues, it is intimately connected to all of them. The Sabbath is the commandment that regulates the human appetite for extraction. It is the institutionalised “pause” – the weekly reminder that neither the human person nor the Earth is a machine whose sole purpose is production. It is the prototype of all sustainable ethics.
Brueggemann’s reading of the Sabbath as a form of resistance against the “Pharaoh” of the market – the ideology of infinite growth and endless productivity – is directly relevant to the crisis of resource imperialism (Brueggemann, p.3). The wars fought over oil and minerals are, at their deepest level, wars fought by societies that have never internalised the Sabbath principle: societies that treat the Earth and its peoples as “standing reserves” of productive resources, to be extracted without limit and without rest. The Sabbath says: stop. The Earth is not yours to consume without end. The people of the land you covet are not yours to exploit. There is a rhythm to the world that must be respected, and the refusal to respect it – the insistence on extraction without pause, production without rest, accumulation without restraint – is not merely morally wrong; it is, as contemporary climate science demonstrates, biologically lethal.
The Quranic parallel – the concept of Mizan (Balance) and the warning against Fasad (Corruption in the Earth) – provides the ecological theology that makes the Sabbath principle cosmically significant. The Quran declares that the balance of the natural order is a divine trust: “And the heaven He raised and imposed the balance, that you do not transgress within the balance” (55:7-8). The industrial plunder of the Earth’s fossil fuels, forests, soils, and biodiversity is, in this framework, a form of cosmic transgression – a violation of the Mizan that sustains all life. Johan Rockstrom’s “Planetary Boundaries” framework provides the scientific quantification of this ancient insight: there are nine “safe operating spaces” for humanity, and we have already breached several of them (Rockstrom, p.472). The Sabbath is the weekly enactment of the recognition that these boundaries exist and must be honoured.
In terms of human well-being, the Sabbath principle aligns with contemporary research in sleep science, chronobiology, and occupational health. Matthew Walker’s research demonstrates that chronic sleep deprivation – the biological equivalent of a violated Sabbath – leads to neurocognitive decline, emotional dysregulation, cardiovascular disease, and suppressed immune function (Walker, p.112). Human beings are not machines. We require periods of genuine rest and non-utility to integrate our experiences, repair our bodies, and renew our capacity for creative and compassionate engagement with the world. The Sabbath is the moral institutionalisation of this biological requirement: a weekly declaration that the human person’s value is not contingent upon their productive output, and that the Earth’s integrity is not contingent upon our willingness to exploit it.
Love as the Fulfilment of the Law: From Prohibition to Possibility
The Ten Commandments, as this paper has argued, are a defensive perimeter against the primary vectors of social destruction: violence, theft, sexual violation, deception, and covetousness. But if moral life were to stop at the level of prohibition, it would produce a society that is at best “stable” – one in which people refrain from harming one another but do not actively invest in one another’s flourishing. The prophetic traditions of all three Abrahamic faiths converge on the insight that the law, in its fullest form, is not merely a set of prohibitions but the expression of a deeper positive imperative: the imperative to love.
Jesus’ synthesis of the entire Law into two commandments – “Love the Lord your God with all your heart… and love your neighbour as yourself” (Matt. 22.37-40) – is the most radical compression of the moral code in the history of ethics. It does not abolish the Decalogue; it fulfils it by identifying the internal disposition from which all genuine compliance with the law flows. If I truly love my neighbour as myself, I will not kill them, steal from them, lie about them, or covet what they have. The law becomes not a constraint imposed from without but an expression of who I have become within.
The Quranic concept of Ihsan – “doing what is beautiful,” the ethics of excellence that goes beyond the minimum required by justice – is the Islamic articulation of the same positive imperative. The Quran presents a tripartite social mandate: “Indeed, God orders justice (Adl), and kindness (Ihsan), and giving to relatives” (16:90). Adl is the floor: the minimum requirement of fairness and non-harm. Ihsan is the ceiling: the commitment to active, generous, creative investment in the flourishing of the other. A society that operates only at the level of justice is a litigious society; a society that operates at the level of Ihsan is a flourishing one. The positive psychology research of Martin Seligman confirms that “prosocial behaviour” – acting for the benefit of others without direct personal reward – is the primary predictor of long-term life satisfaction (Seligman, p.180).
Isaiah Berlin’s distinction between “Negative Liberty” (freedom from interference) and “Positive Liberty” (freedom to realise one’s potential) provides the political philosophy framework for this transition (Berlin, p.121). The Ten Commandments, in their prohibitive form, deliver Negative Liberty: they clear the ground of the primary obstacles to human flourishing. The Love Commandment and the principle of Ihsan deliver Positive Liberty: they provide the energy, the motivation, and the vision that allow human potential to unfold in the cleared ground. Liberation is not merely the absence of oppression; it is the presence of genuine possibility. And genuine possibility requires not only that we stop doing the things that harm our neighbours but that we start doing the things that help them flourish.
Martha Nussbaum’s “Capabilities Approach” – the philosophical framework that measures justice by the actual ability of persons to function and flourish across a range of central human capabilities – provides the contemporary humanistic expression of this vision (Nussbaum, p.33). A just society is not merely one in which people are protected from murder, theft, and deception; it is one in which people have the real capabilities to live long and healthy lives, to access education and meaningful work, to participate in political life, to experience emotional and relational fulfilment, and to exercise the full range of their distinctively human capacities. The Decalogue protects these capabilities from their primary threats. The Love Commandment and Ihsan activate them, sustain them, and invest in their deepest development.
Toward a Global Covenant of Justice, Peace, and Flourishing
The synthesis of all the foregoing arguments points toward a single, integrated vision: the “Global Covenant of Flourishing” – a universal social contract grounded in the ancient moral wisdom of the Decalogue and its parallels, validated by the most current findings of the human sciences, and expressed in the institutional forms appropriate to a deeply interconnected world. This covenant is not a utopian dream. It is a biological necessity for a species that has developed the technological power to destroy itself but has not yet developed the moral maturity to prevent doing so.
The Quranic declaration that all of humanity has been created from a “Single Soul” (Nafsin Wahidah) (4:1) is the foundational ontological statement of this covenant. It asserts that the person on the other side of the conflict, on the other side of the border, on the other side of the theological dispute, is not a stranger but a member of the same fundamental community of being. This is not a sentimental claim; it is a biological reality. Genetic science confirms that the human species is, on the relevant timescale, extraordinarily homogeneous: the diversity we observe at the surface level of ethnicity and culture conceals a profound unity at the level of our shared genetic heritage. The “Single Soul” paradigm is, in this sense, good evolutionary biology.
In practical terms, the Global Covenant of Flourishing requires the institutionalisation of the moral imperatives this paper has analysed:
Against killing and warfare: the reinforcement of international humanitarian law, the consistent prosecution of war crimes in genuinely independent international tribunals, and the sustained diplomatic investment in the resolution of conflicts before they escalate to mass violence. The Sixth Commandment’s prohibition of murder must be given institutional teeth adequate to the scale of contemporary military technology.
Against resource theft and economic looting: the reform of the international financial architecture to ensure “full measure and weight in justice” (Quran 6:152) – transparent contracts, equitable revenue sharing, the cancellation of odious and unjust debts, and the recognition that the natural resources of a people are held in trust for the full development of their capabilities, not for the enrichment of foreign powers or domestic elites.
Against the rape of women in war: the consistent and vigorous prosecution of sexual violence as a war crime and a crime against humanity; the full implementation of the UN Security Council resolutions on Women, Peace and Security; and the transformation of military command cultures to eliminate the conditions of impunity that make mass sexual violence possible.
Against diplomatic deception: the strengthening of the institutions of international transparency – free press, independent monitoring bodies, open-source intelligence – and the development of genuinely accountable multilateral mechanisms for the verification of state claims and the enforcement of international commitments.
Against religious fanaticism and fundamentalism: not the suppression of religion, but its reclamation from the war-mongers and extremists who have colonised it. The humanistic traditions within every faith – the tradition of Al-Ghazali and Ibn Rushd in Islam, of Francis of Assisi and Thomas Aquinas in Christianity, of Maimonides and Abraham Joshua Heschel in Judaism – must be amplified, supported, and given the institutional platforms they need to speak to their communities with the authority of authentic tradition against the distortions of violent extremism.
The philosopher Kwame Anthony Appiah’s concept of “Cosmopolitanism” – the recognition that we have obligations to all human beings, not merely to our fellow citizens – provides the contemporary philosophical expression of the Quranic “Global Ummah” (Appiah, p.12). In a world in which climate change, pandemics, and financial instability respect no borders, the “nationalist idolatry” that locates all moral obligation within the boundaries of the nation-state is not merely morally inadequate; it is biologically dangerous. The destiny of the human species is shared. We will flourish together, as the Quranic single soul working toward a collective Eudaimonia, or we will suffer together the consequences of our collective refusal to do so.
The science of cooperation provides the empirical ground for this hope. Robert Axelrod’s landmark study of the “Iterated Prisoner’s Dilemma” demonstrates that in repeated interactions over time, the most successful strategy is not aggressive self-interest but “Tit for Tat with Forgiveness” – a strategy that begins with cooperation, responds to betrayal in kind, but is always willing to return to cooperation when the other party demonstrates willingness to do the same (Axelrod 27). This is the scientific counterpart to the Quranic command to “repel evil with that which is better” (41:34) and to Jesus’s call for reconciliation and forgiveness. The path to durable peace is not the domination of the powerful over the weak; it is the construction of robust systems of mutual accountability in which cooperation is reliably rewarded and betrayal is reliably discouraged.
The Straight Path Forward
This paper has argued that the Decalogue – interpreted through a humanistic lens and read in dialogue with the Quranic ethical corpus and the teachings of Jesus – provides the most enduring and comprehensive moral argument against the defining crimes of contemporary warfare and international disorder: killing, looting, oil theft, rape, and diplomatic deception. It has further argued that this moral architecture is not merely an ancient religious document but a sophisticated, scientifically validated set of conditions for human biological and social flourishing – conditions that the latest findings of neuroscience, evolutionary biology, social psychology, and peace studies consistently confirm and elaborate.
The war-monger who invaded another nation for its resources has violated the Sixth and Eighth Commandments simultaneously: he has murdered and stolen. The military commander who permits or orders the rape of women has violated the Seventh Commandment and the Quranic principle of Karama – the inherent dignity of every child of Adam. The diplomat who fabricates the pretexts for war has violated the Ninth Commandment and the Quranic imperative of Qist – impartial justice even against one’s own side. The religious fanatic who kills in the name of God has violated the First, Second, and Third Commandments simultaneously: he has made his own will into a god, worshipped an idol of his own ideological construction, and taken the name of the divine in the most catastrophic vain possible. The corporate and state actors who plunder the natural resources of weaker nations have violated the Eighth Commandment and the Quranic principle of Khilafa – the stewardship that we owe to the Earth and to future generations.
Against all of these, the Decalogue speaks with an authority that is simultaneously ancient and urgently contemporary. It speaks not as the property of any single religious tradition but as the moral grammar of the species – the earliest articulation, in the language available to the ancient world, of the conditions under which human beings can live together without destroying one another. It speaks from the Exodus preamble’s insistence that human beings are, first and last, free subjects rather than instruments of another’s will. It speaks from the Quranic single soul’s assertion that every human life is a universe, and its destruction a crime against the whole. It speaks from Jesus’s synthesis of the entire law into the single imperative of love – love that is not a sentiment but a practice, not a feeling but a discipline, not a private devotion but a public commitment to the flourishing of every neighbour, however near or far.
In the year 2026, the foundations of human liberation are not hidden. They are written in our oldest moral texts, confirmed by our newest scientific findings, and echoed in the deepest biological architecture of our evolved social nature. The question before humanity is not whether we have the moral knowledge to build a just and peaceful world. We do. The question is whether we have the moral will to enact it: to dethrone the idols of national interest, racial supremacy, religious exclusivism, and unchecked greed that demand the sacrifice of our neighbours upon their altars, and to choose instead the “Straight Path” of justice, truth, and love.
The Decalogue was given to a community of former slaves as they stood at the threshold of a new existence, free from the logic of Pharaoh for the first time. It was given not as a burden but as a gift: the moral framework within which genuine freedom becomes possible. In 2026, we stand at a similar threshold. The crises that surround us – climate collapse, military expansionism, mass sexual violence, information warfare, the rise of authoritarian fanaticism – are all symptoms of the same underlying failure: the refusal to honour the conditions of our own flourishing. The Decalogue, read humanistically and scientifically, tells us what those conditions are. It remains for us to meet them. The path is straight. The question is whether we will walk it.

title: Liquor ban @10: Welfare drive faces fiscal strain
article_text:
Patna: April 2026 marks exactly 10 years since Bihar enforced one of the country’s most stringent prohibition laws, imposing a complete ban on the manufacture, sale and consumption of liquor. Rolled out by then CM Nitish Kumar in April 2016 as a promise to women voters, the move sought to improve public health, strengthen household finances and curb domestic violence. Ten years on, the ban remains deeply polarising — a policy hailed for social transformation but criticised for economic strain and enforcement hurdles.
For the architects of prohibition, the biggest dividend lies in the improved well-being of vulnerable sections. Research published in ‘The Lancet’ and studies by the International Food Policy Research Institute highlight measurable gains in public health and safety. The ban is credited with preventing nearly 21 lakh cases of intimate partner violence, including a 4.6% decline in emotional abuse and a 3.6% drop in sexual violence against women.
The data further suggests the policy prevented around 24 lakh instances of regular liquor consumption. 
An estimated 18 lakh men avoided becoming overweight or obese due to reduced liquor intake. In rural households, spending patterns also shifted, with money once “splurged” on liquor redirected towards food, education and essential needs. Studies found improved protein consumption and better-quality edible oils, signalling a tangible rise in living standards.
“Initial years saw a notable dip in specific violent crimes, including a 66.6% drop in kidnapping for ransom and a 28.3% decrease in murder cases,” according to a study by the Asian Development Research Institute (ADRI).
However, beneath these gains lies a steep economic cost. What was once a robust revenue stream has turned into a persistent fiscal gap.
Before prohibition, Bihar earned about Rs 3,142 crore annually from excise duties. Over a decade, cumulative losses are estimated to have crossed Rs 30,000 crore. Political critics, particularly from Jan Suraaj, claim the state forfeits nearly Rs 20,000 crore every year — resources they argue could have been used to “establish a world-class education system or fund critical infrastructure.”
In the vacuum created by the ban, an extensive illegal network has flourished. Estimates indicate a parallel liquor economy worth Rs 25,000 crore to Rs 30,000 crore. Despite strict laws, access to liquor remains far from eliminated. A survey in the Patna Municipal Corporation area found 57.8% respondents believed liquor was still available, often at nearly double the earlier price.
Meanwhile, neighbouring states such as West Bengal and Jharkhand have witnessed a surge in excise revenues, fuelled by cross-border purchases.
The enforcement burden has also been immense. The “dry law” continues to strain administrative and judicial systems with enforcement often falling short of intent. Around 17% of men are still reported to consume alcohol.
By 2026, prohibition-related cases have clogged the courts. Earlier estimates indicated over 3 lakh pending cases, prompting sharp judicial criticism. Former Chief Justice of India N V Ramana described the Bihar Prohibition and Excise Act, 2016, as a law framed with a “lack of foresight”. Speaking in Vijayawada in Dec 2021, he observed the Act imposed an “additional burden on courts”, particularly flooding the Patna high court with bail pleas.
Since 2016, over 16 lakh arrests have been made and nearly 10 lakh cases registered under the law. Critics, including Union minister Jitan Ram Manjhi, argue enforcement disproportionately affects the poor, with more than 50% of those jailed belonging to weaker sections while the “mafia” operates largely unchecked.
“The prohibition law has become a curse for the poor. Rich people manage to procure liquor secretly, but it is the poor who get caught,” Manjhi, Union minister and NDA ally, said this many times.
Weak enforcement has also triggered the rise of spurious liquor, particularly in rural areas, leading to repeated hooch tragedies. Over the decade, hundreds have died due to methanol poisoning, compelling the state govt to restore compensation of Rs 4 lakh to victims’ families.
Another troubling fallout has been the growing use of synthetic “dry drugs” among the youth as alternatives to alcohol. A study found over 25% of habitual drinkers shifted to substances such as ganja, charas and synthetic drugs.
As Bihar steps into the second decade of prohibition, political unity on the issue is beginning to crack. While women’s groups remain steadfast supporters, NDA allies and opposition leaders are increasingly calling for a “recalibration” or a “detailed review” of the policy.
Despite mounting pressure, CM Samrat Choudhary has stood firm, ruling out any relaxation. Speaking on Friday, Samrat made his position clear.
“Who will dare to lift the liquor ban which was enforced by a personality like Nitish Kumar and appreciated by Prime Minister Narendra Modi?” Samrat said during an informal interaction with reporters.
As the debate intensifies, the central question persists — will Bihar move towards a regulated model like Gujarat or continue with its uncompromising stance?

title: Trump orders blockade of ‘sanctioned’ Venezuela oil tankers
article_text:
United States President Donald Trump on Tuesday ordered a blockade of sanctioned oil vessels heading to and leaving Venezuela.
The decision escalates Washington’s military and economic pressure campaign on the Nicolás Maduro government in Venezuela. The South American country’s economy is heavily dependent on oil export.
Trump said that Venezuela had been “completely surrounded by the largest armada ever assembled in the history of South America”, adding that “it will only get bigger”.
Since late August, the US has put together a major military deployment off the Venezuelan coast with the stated goal of combatting drug trafficking in Latin America, but has focused on Venezuela.
On Tuesday, the US president said that his country wanted to regain oil that he claimed had been stolen by Venezuela.
“…the shock to them [Maduro government] will be like nothing they have ever seen before – until such time as they return” to the US “all of the oil, land and other assets that they previously stole from us”, Trump said on social media.
It was unclear what oil or land Trump was referring to. Venezuela had nationalised its oil and gas industry in the 1970s.
“The illegitimate Maduro regime is using oil from these stolen oil fields to finance themselves, drug terrorism, human trafficking, murder and kidnapping,” the US president said.
For these reasons, the US was designating the Maduro government as a Foreign Terrorist Organisation, Trump said, adding that he was ordering a “total and complete blockade of all sanctioned oil tankers going into, and out of, Venezuela”.
The US, Canada and several European countries do not recognise Maduro as the Venezuelan president. The countries have for long backed the Venezuelan Opposition.
While Venezuelan oil has faced US sanctions for more than a decade, Caracas has circumvented the measures by selling oil at discounted rates in the black market.
On Tuesday, the Maduro government said that Trump’s actions were aimed at “stealing the riches that belong to our homeland”, AFP reported.
Tensions have escalated in recent weeks after Trump signalled his intention to launch military action inside Venezuela.
On November 30, the US president had unilaterally announced that the Venezuelan airspace should be considered closed. On December 10, the US military seized an oil tanker off the Venezuelan coast, claiming that the vessel was transporting sanctioned oil from Venezuela and Iran.
The US’ military deployment in the Caribbean, meant to combat drug trafficking, includes the country’s largest aircraft carrier strike group USS Gerald R Ford and the advanced F-35 fighter jets.

title: Maharashtra Elections 2024: Maratha-OBC Division Likely To Tilt Scales In Marathwada's Parli, Beed
article_text:
Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar: Maharashtra agriculture minister Dhananjay Munde will have to effectively counter the Maratha vote consolidation in Parli assembly segment, the hometown of late Gopinath Munde which interestingly won't have a BJP nominee in the fray after decades.
Elections to Maharashtra assembly will be held on November 20 and votes will be counted three days later.
Just four months ago, the Maratha factor contributed to the narrow defeat of BJP candidate Pankaja Munde, cousin of Dhananjay, from the Beed Lok Sabha constituency which includes the Parli constituency.
Will Mahayuti Retain Parli Seat
The Maratha quota sentiment remains a strong factor to reckon with in Parli, a rural constituency dominated by issues like MSP for soybean crops and unemployment.
Political observers feel Dhananjay will have to ensure the support of the OBC community to blunt the resentment in Marathas against the BJP-led government.
In a strategic move, Sharad Pawar has fielded Rajesaheb Deshmukh as NCP (SP) nominee against Dhananjay Munde, an Ajit Pawar loyalist and NCP candidate.
Parli is the hometown of the late Gopinath Munde, credited for expanding BJP's footprint in the Marathwada region.
With BJP nominating Pankaja as an MLC and Dhananjay already a member of the NCP camp, the Parli constituency won't have a BJP representative this time.
Pankaja Munde had scored two victories in Parli in 2009 and 2014 polls. She missed a hat-trick in 2019 when Dhananjay Munde defeated her by 30,701 votes.
The brother and sister duo have buried their differences over the last five years.
NCP (SP) nominee Deshmukh claimed Dhananjay had failed to resolve farmers' issues in Parli. He alleged local people are living in an atmosphere of fear and insecurity.
Dhananjay, however, feels that the intensity of the Maratha factor has reduced over the months.
Will Maratha Agitation Show Effects In Beed
Speaking to PTI, he said the caste politics witnessed in the Lok Sabha elections was an aberration, highlighting the victory of candidates of various castes from the Beed parliamentary constituency in the past.
He acknowledged that Beed is not unaffected by Maratha quota agitation, without mentioning reservation leader Manoj Jarange.
"My fight for Maratha reservation was not considered during Lok Sabha polls. Reservation was not the only issue. There are other factors including a limited discontent among farmers," Dhananjay said analysing the Lok Sabha poll outcome.
"The intensity of the quota agitation that existed in general elections has decreased," he claimed.
Queried on whether Beed district witnessed maximum suicides by farmers, the minister listed various initiatives undertaken by the agriculture ministry headed by him.
"The government has paid the insurance premium for farmers. I have also demanded that the import duty on soybean oil be raised. The government has also started centres for purchasing soybeans from farmers," he added.
Sharad Pawar-led NCP (SP) is confident to maintain the momentum it got in the recent general elections. NCP (SP) candidate Bajrang Sonawane had defeated Pankaja from Beed by a thin margin of around 6,000 votes.
The consolidation of Maratha votes in favour of Sonawane is evident as the BJP and the NCP (SP) each had secured the lead from three out of six assembly segments under the Beed parliamentary seat.
Deshmukh said he would establish the rule of law if elected from Parli.
He alleged local businessmen are relocating as fake offences are being registered.
When asked about Pankaja securing a lead in votes from the Parli assembly constituency, Deshmukh said Lok Sabha and assembly elections are distinct.
"Factors like Pankaja Munde's work and sympathy for being Gopinath Munde's daughter benefited her. On the contrary, Dhananjay Munde had betrayed Gopinath Munde. Dhananjay has done no work. Farmers are awaiting payment of crop insurance for years," he claimed.
What Residents Say
Parli resident Chetan Saundale feels the Maratha quota issue won't affect the electoral outcome.
Being a guardian minister of Beed district, Dhananjay Munde has sanctioned an MIDC, a soybean research centre and an agriculture college, though implementation of these decisions is awaited, Saundale said, rejecting the opposition's allegations that Dhananjay is not accessible to common people.
A journalist from Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar, Bipin Deshpande, originally from Parli, feels Dhananjay may face a setback in elections.
"NCP (SP) nominee Deshmukh wields a clout in around 40 villages from the Ambajogai belt. Being an MVA candidate, he can secure significant votes in Parli city," he said.
Importantly, Deshmukh is connected with the Maratha quota agitation and visited its ground zero, Antarwali Sarati village in Jalna district, numerous times to express solidarity with Jarange, Deshpande added.
"Dhananjay Munde's electoral success depends on deft handling of cadres of three constituents of Maha Vikas Aghadi," he said.
Ashwin Mogarkar, a resident of Parli told PTI that BJP workers are dejected as the saffron party has not fielded a candidate- since the seat was allocated to Mahayuti ally NCP - after 44 years.
He said Parli will not be insulated from the Maratha quota protest and the "Jarange factor".
"The Maratha issue and loyal voters of BJP will play a key role in deciding the next MLA of Parli," he added.

title: Asian stocks fall as optimism fades, US bonds hold gains
article_text:
Stocks opened lower in Japan and South Korea. A gauge of global stocks and the S&P 500 Index both posted their first declines of 2026 on Wednesday. Samsung Electronics Co. fell 1.5% even after quarterly profit more than tripled to a record high on global demand for AI servers.
Treasury 10-year yields fell three basis points to 4.15% Wednesday after data showed signs of weakness in US employment, which kept alive bets for at least two Federal Reserve interest-rate cuts this year. Gold and silver steadied after falling for the first time this week.
“The data flow overnight was relatively mixed and that manifested as a mixed session on global markets,” Kyle Rodda, a senior analyst at Capital.com, wrote in a note. “The macroeconomic data also added to the choppiness on Wall Street.”
The moves were a sign the optimism that has boosted risk assets since the start of the year may be starting to wane in the face of rising geopolitical uncertainty and a mixed outlook for the global economy. A busy calendar awaits traders this week, with Friday’s US payrolls report coinciding with a Supreme Court ruling on President Donald Trump’s global tariffs.
Global affairs remained in focus Wednesday as US forces seized two more sanctioned oil tankers as part of its energy quarantine of Venezuela. European leaders closed ranks behind Denmark as President Donald Trump amplified threats to seize Greenland.
Elsewhere, China started an anti-dumping probe into a key chipmaking material from Japan, escalating a dispute between Asia’s largest economies.
In commodities, copper slid from a record high Wednesday, declining along with other industrial metals, as traders booked profits from a swift run-up in prices. Futures for copper, nickel and zinc declined more than 2% at the close of trading on the London Metal Exchange.
Oil edged higher amid more measures from the US regarding Venezuela, including a plan to indefinitely control future crude sales and the seizure of two more sanctioned tankers.
