title: Sixty Days After: Who Won the War?
article_text:
“A whole civilisation will die tonight, never to be brought back again. I don’t want that to happen, but it probably will. However, now that we have Complete and Total Regime Change, where different, smarter, and less radicalised minds prevail, maybe something revolutionarily wonderful can happen, WHO KNOWS? We will find out tonight, one of the most important moments in the long and complex history of the World. 47 years of extortion, corruption, and death will finally end. God Bless the Great People of Iran!” – Donald Trump, Truth Social, April 7, 2026, on day 38 of the war.
In asymmetric warfare, survival against a superior adversary is itself victory– The idea resonating with arguments of asymmetric warfare like Andrew Mack in his influential 1975 essay Why Big Nations Lose Small Wars.
February 11, 2026. The White House Situation Room. The black S.U.V. carrying Prime Minister Netanyahu arrived at the White House just before 11 a.m. The Israeli leader, who had been pressing the United States for months to agree to a major assault on Iran, was whisked inside quickly. Inside the Situation Room, Netanyahu presented “a comprehensive strategy” against Iran. Behind him, on large screens, appeared Mossad chief David Barnea and senior Israeli military officials, reinforcing the image of a coordinated wartime leadership.
Times reconstructed Netanyahu’s arguments. It had four pillars: Iran’s missiles could be destroyed in weeks; the regime couldn’t close the Strait of Hormuz; street protests would resume and, with Mossad help, could produce regime change; and Kurdish fighters could open a ground front from Iraq. He played for Trump a brief video montage of potential new leaders who could take over the country if the hard-line government fell, including Reza Pahlavi, the exiled son of Iran’s last Shah.
Trump responded: “Sounds good to me.”
What happened next? Jonathan Swan and Maggie Haberman, two of the most credible White House correspondents in American journalism, reported in the New York Times.
The following day, February 12, with Netanyahu gone, CIA Director John Ratcliffe convened a private meeting of Trump’s inner circle to present the American intelligence community’s view of Netanyahu’s four-part plan. The assessment is this: Two of Netanyahu’s goals were considered realistic- targeting Iran’s leadership and degrading its military capabilities. The other two – a popular uprising and regime change – were dismissed as detached from reality. CIA Director John Ratcliffe was blunt. Regime change scenarios are “farcical”, said he. Secretary of State Marco Rubio was direct: “In other words, it’s bullshit.” Vice President JD Vance was the only person in Trump’s inner circle to oppose the plan and make a strong case against it.
And yet – Trump went to war anyway. Trump had Venezuela back in his mind. Once the leadership is gone, it was a cake walk, his cronies argued. Trump rejoiced.
Sixty days have now passed since February 28, 2026, when the United States and Israel launched Operation Epic Fury, an ambitious American military assault in the Middle East since the 2003 invasion of Iraq. In twelve hours, nearly 900 strikes rained down on Iranian nuclear facilities, pounded military bases, and pulverised government buildings. Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei was assassinated on the very first day. Dozens of senior officials, generals, and scientists were killed in the rain of missile attacks. Donald Trump promised that the war would last “four weeks or less”. And assured his allies that the war would end in Iran’s “unconditional surrender”.
What was the outcome in these two months?
The Strait of Hormuz is still effectively closed. Talks are stalled in Islamabad. Three US aircraft carrier groups are parked in the Gulf, with no clear pathway home. The ceasefire announced on April 8, 2026, brokered by Pakistan, remains desperately fragile. Will the talks resume? No one knows. What is certain is this: every stated American objective, the denuclearisation of Iran, regime change, control of the Strait of Hormuz, and Iran’s “unconditional surrender”, has failed utterly.
Why Iran Has Won And Trump Has Lost: Ten Reasons
1 Obliteration of Iran’s Nuclear capabilities
The entire stated casus belli of this war was the destruction of Iran’s nuclear programme. The mission has clearly failed.
Let us start with Trump’s boast, as it could complete the exposure.
In June 2025, when strikes on Iran’s nuclear facilities concluded (Operation Midnight Hammer), Trump announced: “It was my great honour to destroy all nuclear facilities & capability. “. Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth went even further than his own commander-in-chief, declaring: “Thanks to President Trump’s visionary leadership .., Iran’s nuclear ambitions have been obliterated.” If the Nuclear facilities were wiped out, where was the need for the present war?
CNN called the most damning proof of a war built on shifting sand. White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt was asked directly why the US might need to strike Iran again, even after its nuclear programme was supposedly “obliterated”. Her answer was: “Well, there are many reasons and arguments that one could make for a strike against Iran.”
When Operation Epic Fury began on February 28, 2026, Trump called the strikes “a spectacular military success”. And said Iran’s key enrichment facilities had been “completely and totally obliterated.” The claims that Iran’s Nuclear capability was “obliterated” were countered swiftly. It was not from Iran or from critics. But from America’s own defence establishment.
Trump launched the war despite the US’s own Director of National Intelligence having testified just a year earlier that Iran was not building a nuclear weapon.
NBC News, citing five current and former US officials familiar with an internal government assessment, reported: One of the three nuclear enrichment sites in Iran struck by the United States was mostly destroyed. But the two others were not as badly damaged, but degraded only to a point where nuclear enrichment could resume in the next several months if Iran wants it to.
US officials knew before the airstrikes that Iran had structures and enriched uranium at Natanz and Isfahan that were safe. And they are beyond the reach of even America’s 30,000-pound GBU-57 “bunker buster” bombs. The Defence Intelligence Agency’s own early assessment concluded, per CNN, that the earlier strikes did not destroy the core components of Iran’s nuclear programme. It only set it back by months.
CSIS, the premier Washington defence think tank, gave the authoritative opinion: Where is Iran’s stockpile of 60 per cent enriched uranium – remains unanswered. After many days of the intensive bombing campaign, the United States does not know where Iran’s highest-enriched uranium is.
Trump laid out four military objectives for the war: destroying Iran’s missile capabilities, annihilating its navy, preventing it from ever obtaining a nuclear weapon and preventing it from arming terrorists. But Secretary of State Marco Rubio contradicted his own colleague Steve Witkoff. He said: Iran was in fact “not enriching right now” – but was trying to restart its nuclear programme in other ways. US intelligence also contradicted Trump. An unclassified Defence Intelligence Agency assessment from the previous year said the prospect of Iran striking the US with an ICBM was still a decade away. And there was no intelligence suggesting this was anything close to an imminent problem.
The single most damning specific fact, stated by Aaron David Miller – former adviser to both Republican and Democratic Secretaries of State and senior fellow at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace – is this: “Stocks of highly enriched uranium – a cornerstone of Iran’s nuclear weapons ambitions – are still under Iranian control.”
His revelation requires no reinforcement: “If the war stopped tomorrow, this constitutes a historic strategic defeat for the US- especially when this was a war of choice.”
And Hegseth’s most infamous operational hyperbole collapsed completely. On March 4, he declared, “Starting last night, and to be completed in a few days, the two most powerful air forces in the world will have complete control of Iranian skies. Uncontested airspace.” Ironically, within weeks, two US fighter jets had been shot down over Iran.
And as Public Broadcasting Service (PBS) News’s expert fact-check concluded: Despite losing many of its top leaders, Iran’s regime remains in charge. The country now exercises unprecedented control over the Strait of Hormuz. Calling it a “total victory” completely ignores the significant strategic setbacks the US has suffered.
March 2025, just a year before the war, US Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard testified that the US intelligence community assessed Iran was “not building a nuclear weapon.” The war was launched on a premise that the US’s own spies publicly disavowed. The Iraq War was launched on this dubious claim: Saddam had biological weapons of mass destruction. Now, Trump has launched the war on specious reasons: Iran has developed Nuclear capability.
2 The Strait Of Hormuz: Iran’s Trump Card
The closure of the Strait of Hormuz is perhaps the single greatest strategic masterstroke in the history of Iranian foreign policy, and it has not been reversed.
Through the Strait passes 20% of the world’s oil. An equivalent share of global liquefied natural gas passes every year. Before the war, roughly 3,000 vessels used it each month. Today, that traffic stands at approximately 5% of pre-war levels (UK House of Commons Library, April 2026). Iran has selectively permitted some ships from “non-hostile” states or those willing to pay Iranian tolls to pass, while blocking others. The effect has been to fracture the Western coalition, to help its allies, China and Russia, and to assert its exclusive rights over the Strait.
Trump demanded that the Strait be opened as a precondition for talks. Iran demanded that the US naval blockade end as a precondition for reopening the Strait. The result is a perfect deadlock in which Iran holds the upper hand. Al Jazeera’s Kimberly Halkett noted from Islamabad, Iran has made clear: “the strait will not be opened to the enemies of this nation through the ridiculous spectacle of the president of the US”.
The Guardian described the situation as a “dual blockade”. The US Navy could blockade Iranian ports, but it had been unable to stop the Iranian blockade or reopen the strait to US allies. That is the strategic picture after sixty days of the most powerful air force in history pounding a country of 88 million people. Iran had definitely won in keeping the Hormuz Strait under its control.
IRGC Political Deputy Brigadier General Yadollah Javani, addressing tens of thousands in Arak, delivered the line that may haunt Washington for a generation: “Today, Iran, which they accused of seeking a nuclear weapon, has achieved a power greater than a nuclear weapon – and that is absolute control over the Strait of Hormuz.” (Al Jazeera)
3 The Catastrophic Economic Toll on the American People
This war is costing the United States an estimated $2 billion a day in direct military costs alone. It is the tip of the iceberg. “I am certain we will spend one trillion dollars for the Iran war,” according to Linda Bilmes.
The Pentagon’s own briefing to Congress confirmed that $11.3 billion had been spent in the first six days. CSIS puts the figure at $16 billion by Day 12. By Day 39, CSIS senior adviser Mark Cancian told National Public Radio that Pentagon budget costs had reached approximately $28 billion, including forces, munitions, aircraft losses, and base damage. The Penn Wharton Budget Model estimates $40 to 95 billion in direct costs, with total economic impact potentially reaching $210 billion (Penn Wharton, March 2026). Linda Bilmes, Harvard Kennedy School professor and one of the world’s foremost authorities on the economics of war, stated bluntly: “I am certain we will spend one trillion dollars for the Iran war.”
The cost asymmetry is grotesque: the US expended interceptors costing 106 times more than the Iranian drones they were shooting down (Iran Cost Tracker, warcosts.org). In the first 48 hours alone, Defence Priorities analyst Jennifer Kavanagh estimated that the US “easily” spent more than $10 billion on air-defence systems.
At the “No Kings” rally in Minnesota on March 28, 2026, before 8 million Americans gathered in over 3,300 cities nationwide, Sanders put a price tag on the lie about the reason for going for a war on Iran: “… At a time when gas prices are soaring, when many Americans cannot afford the necessities of life, it is estimated that this war has already cost us a trillion dollars. .. End This War!”
Gas prices across America jumped nearly 27 cents in a single week, the fastest weekly increase since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022. The 30-year mortgage rate climbed to 6.38% (March 26). American families are paying the bill daily at the gas pump, the grocery store, and the housing market.
The Pentagon is already requesting a $200 billion supplemental appropriation from Congress. Trump has proposed a 50% increase in the defence budget, which, if enacted, would push US military spending to levels 20% higher than the peak of World War II. And all of this is being borrowed at higher interest rates, on top of a $36 trillion national debt, on which the annual interest payments alone are $1 trillion, surpassing the US defence budget.
Many Americans believe that it was Israel that thrust the war on the US to go along with it. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, later, in a separate interview, disclosed that The Intercept called an admission that the US was “forced into war by Israel”.
But appearances are often deceptive. Operation Epic Fury is not a Trump impulse or an Israeli manipulation, but the culmination of 47 years of American determination to reverse the humiliation of 1979 – every war, sanction, and assassination since the Iranian Revolution has pursued a single goal: restoring imperial control over the Persian Gulf.
4 Regime Change: Iran’s Strategic Resilience
When Supreme Leader Khamenei was assassinated on Day 1, Washington and Tel Aviv believed that decapitation of the state head would induce collapse. The opposite happened.
Iran launched strikes across all six Gulf Cooperation Council member states, targeted US bases in Bahrain, Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Jordan, and the UAE, and even allegedly attempted to strike the joint US-UK base at Diego Garcia in the Indian Ocean more than 2,400 kilometres away. The Islamic Republic, battered, leadership-assassinated, internet-blacked-out, and under the heaviest bombing since the 1980-88 Iran-Iraq War, has not surrendered. It has not collapsed. It has not opened the Strait. After sixty days, it retains control of the world’s most important shipping chokepoint. That can never be the portrait of a defeated nation.
Iran rallied the people. People stood with the regime. The IRGC issued a detailed statement declaring it had conducted 22 waves of Operation True Promise III, pressuring “the enemy to call for a ceasefire.” Iran’s National Security Council announced it had “shattered the enemy’s primary strategic goal.” Foreign Minister Araghchi and other officials signalled that Iran might now withdraw from the Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT) in a defiant tone.
The aim was not to annex Iran. The US wants the oil like it is doing in Venezuela.
Costas Lapavitsas, professor of economics at SOAS University of London, explains in his January–February 2026 article in New Left Review – “A Topography of the New Dollar Imperialism” – that appeared just weeks before the bombs fell, as if written as the war’s analytical preface.
He says: For years, sanctions and dollar exclusion strangled the Iranian economy. Then, in 2025 and 2026, came open war launched by the US and Israel. But the aim is not to annex territory or create a colonial administration. Rather, it is to shatter the Iranian state, control its oil resources, and create an obedient vassal of the global system. This is contemporary imperialism in practice: first coercion based on the dollar and the balance sheet, then raw military violence, but not the burden of direct rule.
As the petro-dollar arrangement became shakier, the US wants to bring it back. How is the petro dollar under challenge? The petrodollar system was established in the 1970s. It was to ensure the major oil producers priced their crude exports exclusively in US dollars. In return, the US provided military support. These oil-rich nations then recycled their dollar surpluses back into US Treasury bonds, giving Washington a permanent source of cheap financing. This 50-year arrangement has cracked visibly. On June 9, 2024, the agreement expired without renewal, empowering the countries tied to the petrodollar arrangement to exchange oil for the Chinese Yuan, Euro, and Indian Rupee. The dollar’s share of global reserves has declined from 71% to about 56% since 2008, while central banks have been buying gold at record levels.
Iran has sold oil in non-dollar currencies since 2012. It faces continuous sanctions and military threats as a result. A clear pattern emerges: Iraq announced euro-only oil sales in 2000 -Saddam was removed three years later. Libya proposed a gold-backed African currency- NATO intervened in 2011. Deutsche Bank economists have warned that the Iran conflict is deepening Iran-China ties and “could be remembered as a key catalyst for erosion in petrodollar dominance, and the beginnings of the petroyuan. Iran’s defiance of the dollar system, and its deepening ties with Russia and China, is not merely a backdrop to this war -it is one of its most powerful hidden causes.
Yes. The days of colonial rule were over. Neocolonialism is the post-WW2 reality.
5 The Chaos Inside The Pentagon
The purge of American military leadership during an active war is unprecedented in modern US history. It has ripped open a Pandora’s box of chinks in the armour.
Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth fired Army Chief of Staff General Randy George by phone on April 2, while the top gun was in a meeting. Hegseth simultaneously fired General David Hodne, head of the Army Transformation and Training Command, and Major General William Green Jr., the Army’s chief of chaplains. On April 23, Navy Secretary John Phelan was also dismissed, becoming the first top military official fired mid-war in the Trump era (Al Jazeera, April 23, 2026).
Former Defence Secretary Leon Panetta made a scathing observation. “When people who have that background, who have that experience, who have that combat experience when they’re dismissed for whatever reason… what happens is that sends a terrible message to our other military commanders that they may not be worth much.” (NPR, April 17, 2026).
While Trump never stopped boasting about his victory from day one, why then these dismissals? What do they indicate?
A poll from the conservative Reagan Institute found that overall public confidence in the US military had declined from 70% in 2018 to roughly 50%, with Democratic confidence crashing to 33% (Christian Science Monitor, April 2026).
6 Trump’s Collapsing Political Authority
The war has accelerated Donald Trump’s political descent into territory historically occupied only by the most discredited of American presidents.
As of April 21, eight of nine polls showed Trump’s approval rating in the 30s. A Reuters-Ipsos poll found 36%, an AP-NORC poll found 33%, and an NBC News poll pegged Trump at a new low of 37% (CNN, April 21, 2026). Trump’s 62% average disapproval rating in the CNN Poll of Polls is higher than at virtually any point since 2017, comparable only to George W. Bush at the nadir of the Iraq War debacle.
Two-thirds of Americans 67% disapprove of Trump’s handling of Iran. His economic approval rating hit a historic low of 31%. His disapproval of inflation now routinely registers around 70% (CNN, April 2026). The war has crystallised every Trump vulnerability: rising costs, confused strategy, civilian casualties, and an absence of any credible exit.
Senator Bernie Sanders introduced two resolutions to block hundreds of millions in military arms sales to Israel, earning the support of 40 Democrats, 85% of the caucus in one vote. Sanders’ statement from the Senate floor was incandescent: “This Trump – Netanyahu war is unconstitutional and violates international law. It endangers the lives of US troops and people across the region. We’ve lived through the lies of Vietnam and Iraq. No more endless wars. Congress must pass a War Powers Resolution immediately.” (Al Jazeera, February 28, 2026).
Senator Chris Van Hollen called it plainly “an illegal, regime-change war.” A group of House Democrats introduced articles of impeachment against Hegseth on April 15, accusing him of abusing power, mishandling classified information, and authorising military action without proper legal authority. Even some Republicans “have expressed concerns that Trump’s comments about Iran could hurt the GOP’s midterm chances” (NBC News, April 15, 2026). The War Powers Act’s 60-day clock for congressional authorisation now fell yesterday, April 29, 2026, with no effort to bring the War to a vote in sight.
7 The Illegal War and Global Ramifications
The IMF said that the war in the Middle East, as it wrote in the April 2026 World Economic Outlook, “has halted this momentum” of global recovery.
The IMF downgraded its forecast for global growth to 3.1% in 2026 from 3.3% in January, which itself was already below 2025’s 3.4% expansion. Global inflation expectations rose to 4.4%, driven by oil and gas prices surging amid disruptions to the Strait of Hormuz (PBS/AP, April 14, 2026). IMF chief economist Pierre-Olivier Gourinchas warned that in a “severe scenario”, if the energy shock spills into 2027 and forces central banks to raise interest rates, global growth could drop to just 2%. “Despite the recent news of a temporary ceasefire,” Gourinchas wrote, “some damage is already done, and the downside risks remain elevated.”
The European Central Bank warned that a prolonged conflict could push Germany and Italy into technical recession. British company Shell warned Europe could face a fuel shortage by April. Chemical and steel manufacturers in the UK and EU imposed surcharges of up to 30% to offset surging feedstock costs. Qatar’s Energy Minister warned that Gulf energy exports might halt entirely if war continued, with oil prices potentially reaching $150 per barrel and the long-term threat of “the collapse of world economies” (Economic Impact of the 2026 Iran War, Wikipedia).
The disruption of sulfur, helium (critical to semiconductors), tungsten (whose price surged by more than 50% in March), and nitrogen from the Gulf has injected supply-chain shocks far beyond the energy sector. The war, as the IMF said, “echoes the 2022 commodity price surge following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, which helped push global inflation to the highest since the 1970s” Now the globe has even fewer buffers. Why should the whole world have to bear the brunt of an illegitimate war?
At home, despite the Centre’s half-truths about LPG and petroleum product stocks, ordinary citizens are feeling the pinch of the war. Many establishments have shut down. Migrant workers are leaving the big cities due to the unavailability of cooking gas, and even where it is available, it has become unaffordable. The queues at fuel stations are growing longer each day.
8 Diplomatic Isolation: The World Walks Away From Washington
In an astonishing reversal of post-1945 American global leadership, the United States stands diplomatically isolated over the Iran war.
The United States entered this war by bypassing the United Nations entirely. The WHO condemned the attacks, and the Secretary-General of Amnesty International said that Trump’s statement “may constitute a threat to commit genocide,” following his Truth Social post threatening to destroy “a whole civilisation.” The founding chief prosecutor of the International Criminal Court, Luis Moreno Ocampo, said the war was comparable to Russia’s war in Ukraine. The Security Council itself became the arena for America’s most humiliating diplomatic exposure. The war produced not one but three UN votes – and the US was unable to achieve a single unambiguous victory in any of them.
The Council on Foreign Relations best summarises Europe’s response in a single sentence: the United States launched a major military operation in the Middle East with little to no consultation with its European allies, while expecting to use their bases and receive their broad support. Once again, European leaders found themselves scrambling to react to a conflict they had neither anticipated nor prepared for.
Spain’s Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez was the most forceful European voice of opposition. Ireland and Slovenia also condemned the US-Israeli action. Pope Leo XIV – the first American-born pontiff – condemned Trump’s threat to destroy “a whole civilisation” as “truly unacceptable”. France’s Emmanuel Macron warned that military action conducted outside international law risks undermining global stability.
Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s comment on April 28 was the most chastising statement from any NATO leader: “The Iranians are clearly stronger than expected, and the Americans clearly have no truly convincing strategy in the negotiations either.” The Economist, in an editorial on March 18, made a remarkable statement -calling on “America’s friends” to “help extricate it from an unlawful war.” The phrase “unlawful war” appearing in The Economist’s pages about a US military operation is without precedent in the publication’s modern history. Canada abstained from joining the US-led war on Iran.
Brazil and Mexico called for diplomacy. Colombia outright condemned the US and Israeli airstrikes. Paraguay joined Argentina in explicitly supporting the action. Argentina’s Javier Milei – Trump’s closest ideological ally in the hemisphere – was Washington’s most enthusiastic Latin American supporter. Cuba and Nicaragua released statements condemning Washington’s actions, with Managua sending condolences for Khamenei’s death.
The CELAC summit in Bogotá on March 22 crystallised the left’s position. Colombian President Gustavo Petro called for an immediate ceasefire in the Middle East to prevent a global economic crisis and “potential world war.” The summit ended, as Al Jazeera reported, with Latin American presidents broadly critical of US actions – a sharp contrast to the hemisphere’s posture during previous American military adventures.
Brazil and China condemned the US and Israeli attacks, India firmly stood with the US and Israel despite the US’s humiliating tariffs and a later arm-twisted trade deal. India’s “strategic silence” towards the US- Israel aggression drew wide condemnation.
Who is walking toward world power centre while Washington stumbles?
China and Russia are the unintended beneficiaries of this war. While America counts its losses, Beijing and Moscow are counting their gains, without firing a single shot at the United States.
Ironically, the Iran war is not merely a bilateral confrontation between Washington and Tehran. It is a proxy assault on China’s most vital energy and trade relationships. Iran is China’s largest oil supplier and a cornerstone of the Belt and Road Initiative. A broken, vassal Iran serves Washington’s imperial design. A sovereign Iran, selling oil in yuan and anchoring China’s corridor to the Middle East, is precisely what Washington cannot tolerate. The bombs falling on Tehran are, in part, aimed at Beijing’s economic architecture.
Russia’s gains are quieter but no less real. The war has consumed America’s strategic attention, its defence budget, and its political will. Ukraine, already abandoned in spirit by a Trump administration indifferent to NATO, is now abandoned in practice. Congress will not fund two wars. The world will not sustain two crises. Russia has effectively been handed a free hand in Ukraine while the world watches Hormuz. Putin did not fire a single missile to achieve this. Iran did it for him – not by design, but by consequence.
The Western alliance itself is the third casualty. Europe was neither consulted nor convinced. NATO, already weakened by Trump’s contempt for collective defence, now watches its most powerful member mired in a war of choice that has delivered nothing but costs. The multipolar world that China and Russia have spent two decades quietly constructing is not arriving because they defeated America. It is arriving because America has chosen to defeat itself.
American decline is not a sudden collapse – it is unravelling for decades. This war has accelerated what is already visible on the horizon: a new imperial axis, where Chinese financial and technological power fuses with Russian military reach to define the emerging world order. This is not multipolarity of a world of sovereign equals and genuine non-alignment. It is the replacement of one hegemony with another, more complex configuration of imperial power centres. The victims of this reordering – in Tehran, in Gaza, in Kyiv, in the Global South – will find no liberation in the transition. Yet, the sharpening of contraditions among the imperiliast powers help the revolutionary and national liberation movements.
True. The world order is changing. The grammar of imperialism is not.
9 THE LEGAL AND MORAL RECKONING
The war has generated a mounting global legal and moral indictment of both the United States and Israel.
The attack was launched while the two sides were in active negotiations, a fact that many legal experts called the most destabilising precedent in modern international law. Gabor Rona, an international law expert who spoke to NPR, stated that Trump’s threats to destroy Iranian civilian power plants, oil wells, and desalination plants constituted “a threat to commit war crimes both under international and US law (NPR, April 2, 2026). The March 7 Red Crescent report documented that 6,668 civilian “units” had been targeted by US-Israeli strikes, including 5,535 residential units, 14 medical centres, and 65 schools.
The killing of 120 schoolgirls in Minab by the Tomahawk missile on the opening day of the war and a US military investigation that confirmed the strike resulted from “outdated targeting data” has become a symbol of the moral catastrophe. At least 15% of all Iranian casualties are under 18 years of age. Middle East Eye reported the use of “double-tap” airstrikes, striking the same location twice to maximise casualties among rescuers, though the US denies this. On MSNBC’s All In with Chris Hayes, Mehadi Hasan called the war “a moral abomination and tactically stupid.” The only morality of the imperialists is greed and profits. Nothing stands before them.
10 The Strategic Insolvency
Wars are won by achieving objectives, not by counting bombs dropped.
Trump set five explicit objectives: Forestall Iran’s nuclear programme, stop Iran’s missiles, prevent a nuclear weapon, seize Iranian oil, and achieve regime change. Not one has been accomplished.
The WSWS captured the essential absurdity: Trump declared that the “objectives” of the war were “dismantling the regime’s ability to threaten America or project power outside of their borders.” Yet this aim has plainly not been achieved – Iran still controls the Strait of Hormuz.
The DIA’s own “low confidence” assessment found the nuclear programme set back by “only a matter of months.” Iran’s missiles continue to fly drones and ballistic missiles have struck American bases in eight countries and reached as far as Diego Garcia. The enriched uranium is entombed underground in facilities the IAEA can no longer access, meaning the nuclear question is now less resolved than before the bombs fell. The oil has not been seized; oil prices have instead risen by more than 55%, costing American consumers billions. And regime change? Iran’s new Supreme Leader, Khamenei’s son, assumed power. The IRGC issued triumphalist communiques. President Pezeshkian called it a “great victory” on national television. Iran sits at the negotiating table in Islamabad not as a supplicant seeking mercy, but as a country with its own five-point proposal, rejecting the American fifteen-point framework, and insisting on sovereignty over the Strait of Hormuz.
Former Sanders foreign policy adviser Matt Duss captured the broader political view in an interview with The Intercept: “A supermajority of Democrats oppose this war, are generally against America’s global military interventions,” and are demanding accountability (The Intercept Briefing, April 17, 2026). Former Harvard Kennedy School economist Linda Bilmes’s conclusion is the most sober: “The Trump administration expected this war would be over quickly and would be relatively inexpensive… it is costing about two billion dollars a day, and that is the tip of the iceberg.”
CSIS analyst Cancian told NPR: “We are sending the bills to our children and grandchildren.” The WarCosts.org analysis states it plainly: the Iran War “seemed destined to join the long list of American military interventions that achieved tactical victories while producing strategic defeats but at a pace and cost that exceeded even the worst projections.”
In Small Wars Journal published April 27, 2026 -just three days ago – Dr. Tahir Mahmood Azad of the University of Reading, introduces a term that may define the era of the US decline:
“The conflict has exposed a condition of American strategic insolvency: a country whose simultaneous commitments in Europe, the Indo-Pacific and the Gulf can no longer be sustained by its depleted arsenal, overstretched budget, or fractured alliances. The immediate military victory the president is claiming cannot mask the structural damage the war has done to the post-Cold War order the United States itself built.”
For America that constructed that order, the writing is on the wall.
A Small Nation Can Defeat A Superpower
Sixty days in, the war was supposed to last four weeks and end in Iran’s unconditional surrender. The war continues undecided, unresolved, and metastasising into a permanent crisis.
The 60-day War Powers Act clock expired yesterday. Congress has not authorised the war. The bombs may fall again.
Iran’s president declared a great victory on national television.
The Trump administration is finding a way out to save its honour and exit, for now.
Yes. A small nation can defeat a superpower in an unjust war. Vietnam did it with sacrifice. Afghanistan did it with time. Iran does it with something no superpower can bomb into submission – the will of a people who have already outlived a hundred empires and are in no hurry to bow before one more.

V Subrahmanyam, Advocate, Guntur

title: Olive oil vs. avocado oil: Benefits, nutrition, and best uses explained
article_text:
When it comes to choosing the right cooking oil, we weigh more than just taste. We ask: Is it heart-friendly? Does it bring nutrients along with flavor? Or is it simply adding fat without value? These questions often surface as we reach for a bottle before sautéing vegetables, tossing a salad, or prepping a stir-fry.
From sunflower and soybean to rice bran and vegetable oil, the market offers plenty of options. But when it comes to combining health benefits with culinary versatility, olive oil and avocado oil are front-runners.
Both are celebrated for their rich stores of heart-friendly monounsaturated fats and valuable antioxidants. Yet they differ in taste, heat resistance, and the amount of research backing their health claims. Olive oil, a Mediterranean staple, brings bold, fruity character and a long history of proven benefits. Avocado oil, mild and buttery, shines when the heat is high.
So, which cooking oil should you choose? That depends on your cooking style, health priorities, and budget. Let’s dive deep and explore the details so that you can find your best fit.
Poll
Which cooking oil do you prefer for everyday use?
Olive oil vs. avocado oil: Nutrition and benefits
What is olive oil?
Olive oil is a golden liquid fat pressed from the fruit of the olive tree. Known as the lifeblood of Mediterranean cuisine, it’s also valued in cosmetics, traditional remedies, and even ancient lamp fuel. 
Nutritionally, it’s prized for its high monounsaturated fat content and polyphenols, powerful plant compounds linked to numerous health benefits. 
What is avocado oil?
Avocado oil comes from the creamy green pulp of the avocado fruit, native to the Persea americana tree. With a naturally high smoke point and delicate taste, it works in everything from searing steaks to blending into salad dressings. Like olive oil, it’s rich in monounsaturated fats, antioxidants, and key nutrients.
Nutrition: Healthy fats and vitamins
Both oils share a nutritional core: monounsaturated fats, especially oleic acid, an omega-9 fatty acid known to reduce bad cholesterol (LDL) and inflammation. Monounsaturated fats are a healthier alternative to saturated and trans fats, according to the 
American Heart Association (AHA). 
Research shows that people who consume more monounsaturated fats have healthier metabolic and cardiovascular health profiles, especially as compared to people who consume large quantities of saturated and trans fats.
Per tablespoon:Olive oil (extra virgin): ~119 kcal, 13–14 g fat, ~9.9 g MUFA, ~1.4 g polyunsaturated, ~1.9 g saturated fat.
Avocado oil: ~124 kcal, 14 g fat, ~9.9 g MUFA, ~1.9 g polyunsaturated, ~1.6 g saturated fat.
The difference is small, but olive oil wins for vitamins E and K, which support antioxidant activity and blood health. Avocado oil generally offers lower amounts of these vitamins.
Antioxidants and unique compounds
Olive oil, especially extra virgin (EVOO), is loaded with polyphenols, phytosterols, chlorophylls, and oleocanthal, a natural anti-inflammatory compound with effects similar to a small dose of ibuprofen, as per 
research. These antioxidants contribute to heart, brain, and digestive health.
Avocado oil brings its own arsenal: chlorophylls, carotenoids, and β-sitosterol, a plant sterol linked to reduced inflammation and potential cancer-protective effects. It also boosts absorption of fat-soluble nutrients like carotenoids from vegetables, making it a smart pairing with salads or roasted veggies.
Smoke point and heat stability
Olive oil (EVOO): Smoke point ~190 °C (375 °F). Best for drizzling, dipping, or low-to-medium heat cooking.
Avocado oil (refined): Smoke point up to 250 °C (482–520 °F). Ideal for high-heat methods like deep-frying, searing, grilling, and roasting.
If your dish needs intense heat, avocado oil handles the pressure without breaking down. For flavor and cold dishes, olive oil takes the crown.
Health benefits
Olive oil’s benefits are backed by decades of research, especially within the 
Mediterranean diet. Regular use is linked to reduced risk of heart disease, dementia, certain cancers, and better cholesterol balance. It’s also known for its anti-inflammatory properties and potential to support longevity.
Avocado oil is newer to the research spotlight but shows promise. Studies suggest it can help with weight management, stabilize blood sugar, improve cholesterol profiles, and lower cardiovascular risk when used in place of saturated fats.
Flavor, cost, and availability
Flavor:Olive oil: Fruity, peppery, sometimes grassy; adds complexity to salads, breads, and finishing touches.
Avocado oil: Mild, buttery, and slightly grassy: blends in without overpowering other ingredients.
Cost:Olive oil (especially EVOO) is generally more affordable and easier to find.
Avocado oil is often pricier and may be less common in smaller stores.
Best uses in the kitchen
Olive oil:Dressings, drizzling, and gentle sautéing.
Ideal for Mediterranean recipes, dipping bread, finishing soups, or topping vegetables for both flavor and nutrition.
Avocado oil:High-heat cooking: frying, searing, grilling, roasting.
Works well in marinades, stir-fries, and baking, where a neutral flavor is preferred.
How to choose
Opt for unrefined or cold-pressed oils; they retain more nutrients and authentic flavor.
Store in a cool, dark place to protect antioxidants and prevent rancidity.
Use both oils strategically: EVOO for raw applications and flavor; avocado oil for heat resilience.
Check quality labels: Some avocado oils on the market are rancid or diluted with cheaper oils. Trusted brands are worth the investment.
The final verdict?
Both olive and avocado oil have unique strengths. Olive oil brings centuries of culinary tradition and proven health benefits; avocado oil offers heat stability and subtle flavor. Keeping both in your pantry ensures you’re ready for any recipe, whether it calls for a gentle drizzle or a sizzling sear.
In case you're looking for something else apart from olive oil and avocado oil, canola oil is a great all-around choice for cooking, especially for high-heat cooking like frying and baking. It has a neutral flavor and a high smoke point, making it versatile. Other good options include sunflower, safflower, and grapeseed oils, which also have neutral flavors and high smoke points. If you're looking for something with a distinct flavor, consider sesame or nut oils, but be mindful of their lower smoke points.

title: Great Nicobar Megaproject: A Looming Linguicide
article_text:
In the long-lost spirit world of the Andamanese, Nila wanders alone, dwelling in anthills. He wields a knife but rarely turns it against humans. His hunger is strange: he feeds not on flesh but on the earth, consuming it endlessly.
Today, at Great Nicobar, a UNESCO Biosphere Reserve, Nila seems to have returned. Not as a mythic spirit but as a ravenous force of development: a Rs.92,000 crore megaproject wrapped in the hollow promises of “holistic development”. In its very first phase, it would swallow 166.10 sq km of the island’s approximately 910 sq km, around 850 sq km of which is protected as a tribal reserve.
Just as Nila’s hunger once knew no bounds, the Great Nicobar megaproject now threatens to consume the island’s ancient forests, pristine lands, fragile coastlines, and the intricate ecosystems that cradle rare and endangered life. It imperils the Nicobarese and the Shompen—two historically isolated indigenous communities who, for millennia, have lived as gentle stewards of this island world. Their resistance to the megaproject is not political but existential.
Much has been written about the environmental, social, and economic toll the Great Nicobar megaproject is likely to exact. Yet, one crucial dimension remains entirely overlooked: its disastrous impact on indigenous languages.
The Nicobarese language family comprises six tongues: Pu, Sanenyo, Luro, Mout, Lamongse, and Takahanyi Lang. Many, especially those spoken in Great and Little Nicobar, survive with only a small number of speakers and are acutely vulnerable to outside pressures.
The Shompen, classified as a Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Group, face an even graver threat. The megaproject will destroy their gipen (forests), gihous (lands), seashores, and the unique flora and fauna that sustain both the community and their culture. Beyond these ecological and cultural losses lie the imminent danger to their ancient language—a linguistic isolate with no known relation to any other tongue or language family. If it disappears before being properly documented, an entire world view, centuries of ecological knowledge, and the intricate semiotics encoded in its structure will be gone.
Also Read | Great Nicobar’s consent con
To truly grasp what is at stake, we must reflect on the following questions: How are languages, cultures, and ecologies intertwined in indigenous life-worlds? In what ways do languages encode ecological knowledge, place-based wisdom, and sustainable ways of living? What vanishes when an indigenous language dies? And how does such erasure impact the collective memory and identity of its speakers?
We are two researchers—an anthropologist and a linguist—who have spent decades studying indigenous communities in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands. We have lived in their villages, walked forest trails with them, witnessed age-old rituals, listened to the last speakers of vanishing tongues, and sat with cultural custodians who carry memories of worlds torn apart: first by the Indian Ocean tsunami of 2004 and then by the calamities caused by culturally insensitive aid efforts.
In their stories—and in their silences—we have traced the unravelling of ancient languages and lifeways. From this long engagement, we carry a deep understanding of how British colonialism and the postcolonial state fractured their worlds, and feel a pressing obligation to speak. Today, the state-driven vision of “holistic development” in Great Nicobar threatens to erase indigenous futures altogether. A linguicide now looms large.
Linguistic, cultural adaptation and resilience
In the indigenous world, language, culture, and ecology are inseparably braided. Of the world’s 36 recognised biodiversity hot spots, most are in regions of extraordinary linguistic diversity. Yet, they remain acutely vulnerable to state policies that privilege extraction over preservation. When these ecosystems are disturbed, their shock waves reverberate through languages and cultures that have coevolved within fragile socioecological systems through adaptation and resilience.
Indigenous communities possess unparalleled ecological wisdom born from an intimate bond with their environments and preserved and expressed through their languages. Take, for instance, the Andaman islanders: the Great Andamanese migrated to these islands from Africa some 70,000 years ago, while the Onge and the Jarawa arrived later, perhaps 50,000 years ago. Their languages carry millennia of survival knowledge, finely attuned to their surroundings and passed down through generations.
On the morning of December 26, 2004, when the Indian Ocean tsunami struck, not a single Andamanese life was lost, even as over 10,000 perished elsewhere in India. Each tribe read signs of the tsunami through its own lexicon of survival. Seeing fish rise from the sea’s twilight zone, the Great Andamanese cried: “Sare-ukku buroko” (the sea has turned upside down). The Onge called it, “giyangejebey” (the land became water). The Jarawa, noting strange wave patterns, instinctively fled to higher ground. Their ancient languages carried the keys to their survival, encoding ecological wisdom that enabled them to recognise the danger before it struck.
But their deep ecological knowledge extends far beyond oral warnings of danger. A comparison of the Great Andamanese bird names with scientific taxonomy reveals remarkable ethno-ornithological expertise: 109 species across 14 orders and 38 families correspond closely with modern classifications. Such alignments testify to a sophisticated, place-based science encoded in language.
Indigenous languages embody an inner lexicon that binds people to the earth and anchors them in place. Deeply intertwined with their local ecologies, these languages preserve knowledge that is geographically grounded and environmentally responsive. In the Luro language of Teressa Island, for instance, multiple spatial deictics—equivalents of “there” in English—precisely situate speaker and referent within their geography: oh for nearby on the island, unya for moderately distant, ung for far on the island or beyond (for example, Port Blair), aut directs towards the southern Nicobar group (for example, Great Nicobar), and au towards the northern group (for example, Car Nicobar). This rich spatial vocabulary reflects not just linguistic complexity but a world view rooted in topography, local knowledge, and a deep sense of place.
Indigenous toponymy among the Great Andamanese adds another layer to this relationship between language and environment. Place names are never arbitrary; they encode ecological observations, hazards, or mythological significance. Maro Phong (honey-cave) identifies a site for wild honey collection; Rait Phor (big bamboo-small bamboo) marks bamboo groves near present-day Mayabunder; Bol Phong (Bol fish-cave) on Long Island recalls the Bol fish, entwined with local myths of abundance and caution.
When British colonisers documented the islands’ place names, they relied on local tribes for guidance. Remarkably, some islanders named places instantly upon first sight, drawing solely on keen observation of topography. The Bea people of southern Great Andaman identified the second highest hill, later called Saddle Point, as Puluga-Chang (the abode of the first man), and Lurua (fire), believed to be the site where fire was first discovered.
Other Great Andamanese groups, such as the Jero, originally coastal dwellers who later relocated to Strait Island, named places according to maritime ecology. Toro-Tec (turtle leaf) marked waters rich in turtle life near Mayabunder; Phocho Toy, named after a local flower, denoted an islet in front of Strait Island; Jiro Tauro (Jiro turtle), an islet near Strait Island, linked sea life directly to clan identity.
Larger islands, too, carried ecological and mythological significance: Tebi-Siro (shores of the open sea) for Neil Island, Boa (land/earth) for Baratang Island, Lurua (fire) for Bluff Island, and Sorobul (the dangerous area) for South Andaman, home of the rival Jarawa tribe. Havelock Island was once called thi-lar-siro (land-turtle-sea), a mnemonic map marking it as an ideal site for turtle hunting.
Such names reveal deep ecological connections. They are not merely descriptive labels but cultural codes that prescribe how spaces are to be used, respected, and remembered. Geography thus becomes cultural ecology, where survival practices intersect with cosmology and collective memory. The indigenous name for Port Blair, Lao-tara-Nyo (house of evils/house of foreigners), illustrates how toponymy encodes historical trauma. It bears witness to colonial disruption while also showing how imposed names—Port Blair and, more recently, Sri Vijaya Puram—overwrite indigenous epistemologies, erasing not only identities but also the living bonds between land, community, and memory.
Vocabularies reflecting the rhythms of daily life
Indigenous languages also encode vocabularies that reflect people’s intimate relations with forests, coastlines, and the rhythms of daily life. The Great Andamanese language, for example, differentiates six types of forest openings (thimikhu). The sea, too, is richly layered, with terms for shifting shorelines (karangik). Hunting unfolds into a precise lexicon: balcho for forest hunting, angol for sea hunting, lara for turtle hunting, shi for big game hunting, baleu for setting out on a hunt, fara for hunting in general, and shitbom for hunting and gathering.
Among the Jarawa, body parts are named after parts of trees, reflecting the belief that humans and trees share the same mother. This relationality surfaces in other indigenous languages as well: in Luro, the Nicobarese language of Teressa Island, chau denotes both “grandparents” and “tree”, while ia means both “father” and “banana plant”.
In the Nicobar Islands, the forest provides the bulk of the resources that sustain life. The islanders hunt, gather timber, tubers, and fruits, and tend orchards along forest edges and coastal zones. Their diet is rooted in local abundance, weaving ecology directly into culinary practice.
The sea is equally vital. The islanders fish using hook and line, cast nets, stationary nets, and canoes. Their maritime expertise is once again embedded in language that encompasses rich vocabularies for marine fauna and flora, net-making, canoe-making, fishing practices, and related phenomena. In Sanenyo, the language of Teressa Island, terms such as hinuak (fishing line), wet (fishing hook), and kanwal (net) exist alongside more than 20 distinct fish names, encapsulating generations of practical skills and ecological understanding.
The islanders also have detailed ecological knowledge of the medicinal uses of the forests, seas, and lands. On Chowra Island, Sanenyo speakers use the leaves of the rai-tachonku tree mixed with coconut oil to treat viral infections. Crushed rai-hangoya leaves blended with rainwater are applied to the forehead to ease headaches. For wounds, both humans and animals are treated with the juice of kati leaves mixed with lime from crushed seashells, a potent antiseptic. The community also produces its own lime and salt, embedding both its healing and culinary practices in locally available resources.
Among medicinal plants, the hua is especially versatile: its sap counteracts snakebites, its powdered bark mends dislocated joints and sprains, and its crushed leaves can temporarily intoxicate fish, making them easier to catch. A related plant, en in the Great Andamanese language, once grew along the Andaman coast but was lost to the 2004 tsunami. Such remedies exemplify the pharmacological wisdom embedded in indigenous languages and lifeways where healing, sustenance, and survival practices are passed down the generations.
For the islanders, the forests are more than sources of subsistence; they are sanctuaries that shape their moral and spiritual order of life. On Chowra Island, the forest’s periphery is open to all, while deeper zones are governed by cultural taboos that protect their sanctity. Movement within these spaces follows codes of dress: plain garments are worn in the inner forest—perhaps to enhance visibility in dim light—while simple, colourful clothing may be worn near the edges. Language, too, marks these boundaries: only the native tongue is spoken upon entry, affirming that to cross into the forest is to step into a realm where land, spirit, and culture converge.
Menchal and Meroë in southern Nicobar, and Tillanchong in central Nicobar, are considered sacred and are governed by strict taboos. Visits are carefully regulated, and every form of life on these islands is protected. For the Nicobarese, these are not mere stretches of land to be exploited but living beings, abodes of powerful spirits whose presence commands respect.
Such reverence for nature among indigenous peoples resonates across India. The Lepchas, indigenous to the Himalayan region, for instance, trace their very origins to Mount Kanchenjunga, linking each of their 108 clans (moo) to the 108 peaks (chyu) believed to be the soul’s final resting place. The Great Andamanese measure time through nature: their calendric system is based on the seasonal blooming of flowers, and newborn girl children are named after the flower in bloom during their birth.
Languages as archives of knowledge
Thus, language serves as a bridge, binding life to land, and weaving culture, ecology, and spirit into an indivisible whole. But what happens when indigenous peoples lose this vital bridge of language? Language, culture, ecology, and life are inseparable, bound together in a single breath. The loss of one inevitably erodes the other. Language is not a neutral conduit; it is an archive of social and ecological relations, world views, knowledge, and wisdom. A language never vanishes in isolation; it dies alongside the worlds it encodes.
Linguistic structures, like DNA, carry traces of the distant past, often holding knowledge unknown even to their speakers. When a language dies, the loss extends far beyond grammar and vocabulary: ecological classifications, ethnobotanical knowledge, calendrical systems, numeracy, navigation techniques, local cosmologies, medicinal practices, spiritual traditions, and more vanish. These systems constitute epistemological frameworks with profound relevance for science, sustainability, and human understanding.
Each language is a mirror of the world in which it was born, reflecting a community’s intimate relationship with its local environment. Through words, stories, myths, oral histories, and traditions, people pass on ecological knowledge, cultural values, and spiritual understandings of the human-nature connection. The Jarawas remind us of this truth: for them, trees and humans share the same mother; to fell a tree is not simply to cut wood but is akin to killing kin. When the forests of Middle Andaman were torn apart in the 1970s to build the Andaman Trunk Road, this ancient spiritual equilibrium was shattered.
Similarly, terms for colours provide striking examples of the human-nature intimacy: desert languages often hold rich vocabularies for browns and greys to capture the subtle variations of sand; Ethiopian languages distinguish multiple shades of green, mapping the many kinds of bamboo in their forests; and the Maya language names nine distinct shades of blue, each after a different butterfly of the Amazon.
When such languages disappear, it is not merely the words that are lost. Centuries of environmental knowledge, sustainable practices, cognitive abilities of fine demarcations, and cultural insights vanish. These are resources that are urgently needed to navigate today’s crises of biodiversity loss and climate change.
The lexical variations among the languages of different communities also reflect distinct ways of thinking, often generating concepts and meanings that are difficult to translate. Every language offers its speakers a unique cognitive lens to perceive the world.
In languages such as Khasi and Jaintia of Meghalaya, the Naga languages of Nagaland, and the Munda languages of Jharkhand, special terms known as “expressives” capture subtle nuances in walking, eating, laughing, crying, and other everyday actions. For instance, Khasi contains 20 distinct expressives for bam (eating), 38 for kirn (speaking), 57 for yam (crying), and 66 for yaid (walking), illustrating its remarkable semantic precision in capturing human actions.
These words do more than describe. They reveal how language encodes a community’s entire cognitive and cultural landscape. When such languages erode or vanish, we lose a way of seeing, interpreting, and engaging with the world and narrow the very horizons of human thought.
Ecological deteriorations strike at the heart of indigenous culture, identity, and world view—all of which are woven into a community’s heritage language. The delicacy of the links between biodiversity, cognition, culture, and linguistic expression means that threats to the environment also imperil the words and concepts that give it meaning. For instance, in Koraput, Odisha, the local language once had hundreds of terms for taste, reflecting the 1,700 varieties of rice traditionally grown and consumed in the region. The Green Revolution homogenised the crop, erasing much of this culinary and linguistic richness. Today, the community retains only three or four words for “taste”, a stark reminder that environmental and agricultural change can constrict both perception and vocabulary.
Similarly, the Mullu Kurumba language, spoken on the Tamil Nadu-Kerala border, once had more than a dozen words for kume (wild mushrooms), with each carrying specific ecological and culinary significance. With the loss of these mushrooms to deforestation and tea plantations, their words too have faded.
Across the world, megaprojects driven by urban-centric visions and vested interests have displaced indigenous peoples, forcing them onto degraded lands and eroding their cultural traditions, languages, and ecological balance.
The history of the Andaman islanders offers a stark cautionary tale. The Great Andamanese, once nearly 5,000 strong and spread across the archipelago, have dwindled to around 50, while the settler population on their lands has now surpassed 4,00,000.
British colonisation in 1858, with forced land seizure and the introduction of alien diseases, devastated both their population and languages. Postcolonial development interventions compounded the tragedy: epidemics, steady erosion of land and forest rights, and forced relocation to Strait Island under the guise of “tribal welfare” completed the cycle of dispossession. Other indigenous groups in the region suffered similarly. Their collective history now reads like an epic of loss, heartbreak, and injustice—a testament to the results of relentless pressures of colonial and postcolonial powers on fragile communities and the enduring ecological knowledge encoded in their languages.
The Great Andamanese language distinguishes two tenses: past and non-past. The past is further divided into three categories—immediate past, remote past, and narrative past—revealing how experiences are recorded, remembered, and transmitted across generations. Forced dislocation has disrupted this delicate system, leaving the indigenes disoriented and compelled to rebuild from scratch. In such upheaval, past experiences and the wisdom they carried have vanished along with social structures, communication patterns, and cultural identity itself.
While among the Jarawa and the Onge, the intergenerational transmission of language continues, preserving culture and knowledge, the Great Andamanese have already witnessed the death of the last speakers of three ancient tongues: Khora, Bo, and Sare. Today, only four elderly speakers of Jero remain, and they struggle to keep it alive.
The precarious future of Great Nicobar life-worlds
The indigenous peoples of Great Nicobar now face a similarly precarious future. Their subsistence economy, their unique ways of life, and their heritage languages will be imperilled by the pressures of the megaproject.
The disastrous impact of the project can be predicted on the basis of the government’s earlier settlement scheme in Great Nicobar. Between 1969 and 1980, the government settled 330 ex-servicemen’s families in 7 villages along the south-east coast, allotting each family around 11 acres of land. Two roads—the North-South Road (51 km) and the East-West Road (43 km)—were constructed, cutting through landscapes that had sustained indigenous lives for generations. The settlements displaced the Shompen people from their ancestral homes, reducing their resource base and turning both the Great Nicobarese and the Shompen into a minority in their own islands.
The Indian Ocean tsunami of 2004 further devastated Nicobar, claiming around 10,000 lives, which is nearly one-third of the archipelago’s population. In Great Nicobar, nine Shompen and hundreds of Nicobarese people perished. In the tsunami’s aftermath, the government evacuated the Nicobarese from their ancestral habitats and resettled them in Rajiv Nagar, Campbell Bay, against their wishes, turning them into internally displaced people. The indigenes have longed to return to their former homes. But their very lands are now earmarked for the megaproject which threatens to make the Nicobarese displacement permanent.
The megaproject will subject the Shompen and the Nicobarese to what the Andaman islanders have already endured: a genocide, an ecocide, and a linguicide. Plans for a “greenfield city” envision hundreds of thousands of outsiders arriving at Great Nicobar. For its indigenous communities, such an influx would mean not only the loss of lands and livelihoods but also the erasure of cultures, languages, and ecological knowledge that they have safeguarded for generations.
The megaproject is a looming linguistic and cultural genocide. Speakers of the Sanenyo language capture the stakes vividly: “If there are no forests, there are no kanyap trees. Without kanyap trees, there can be no hodi [canoe]. Without hodies, there will be no sailors, and our knowledge of seafaring and canoe-building will be lost forever.”
These canoes, designed for one to several people, are central to fishing and navigation. Their loss would erase indigenous craft and ancient oral traditions, including songs, festivals, rituals, and dances that accompany boat-making and recount adventures at sea. These practices, which nurture children from an early age, form the cultural heartbeat of the community; their disappearance would leave an irreplaceable void.
The indigenous languages of Great Nicobar are especially rich repositories of traditional knowledge of local plants, herbs, creepers, and remedies for ailments ranging from seasickness to malaria to orthopaedic conditions. Over a long time, the people have fostered resilient ecosystems that sustained culturally significant foods, wildlife, medicinal plants, and sustainable subsistence economies. For millennia, they have thrived self-sufficiently, living in deep harmony with the forest and its intricate ecology. The seashore and marine resources are equally vital, shaping cultural, social, and emotional worlds.
Also Read | Mathias calls it ‘the death of life’
Stripping the people of these familiar environments and ancestral resources risks forcing their dependence on outsiders and eroding their dignity and self-worth. Ultimately, it poses a pressing question: can any form of development ever replicate the harmonious human-nature equilibrium these communities have perfected over countless generations?
Language, particularly, anchors identity, nurtures self-esteem, and strengthens social and ecological cohesion. Research shows that revitalising indigenous languages can boost mental health, lower suicide rates, and reduce chronic diseases. Conversely, its erosion fuels addiction, alienation, and intergenerational trauma, as the Great Andamanese experience so starkly demonstrates.
Preserving language is inseparable from preserving life itself. The extinction of ancient tongues such as Shompen or Nicobarese will not merely amount to cultural attrition but to the obliteration of unique cognitive systems vital for grasping the spectrum of human intelligence.
Language diversity illuminates humanity’s evolutionary journey, revealing the breadth of cultural and ecological adaptations. Once lost, languages—like coral reefs or old-growth forests—do not regenerate. Their disappearance constrains the world views and practical tools available for navigating a rapidly changing planet.
It is a harsh truth that we must confront: to kill a language is to rob the earth of its voices.
Ajay Saini, an anthropologist, teaches at the Centre for Rural Development and Technology, IIT Delhi. Anvita Abbi, a linguist, serves on the Expert Committee of the UNESCO World Atlas of Languages and is former professor and chair of the Centre for Linguistics at JNU, Delhi.
